She should explain to the Archbishop why she wishes to come to Piacenza and trust in his kindness and understanding. She should buy nothing, but bring the lace and the chasuble.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Although I am immersed in work, I did not want to have others write, so that I could answer you in my own hand.

2. You tell me the Archbishop does not want you to leave.1 Listen, when you have settled the sisters well, then you can tell the Archbishop that you urgently need to come and confer with me; that, having nothing to do for the moment, you would make a quick trip here; moreover that I had promised it to you;2 and that you would make the journey in haste with the sole purpose of coming back, because you really need it.

3. You will see that he is so good that I have no doubt he will grant you this favour. He is a most charitable Father.

4. Listen, do not buy anything, because I n...3 and for now it is not possible; you can do it on another occasion. So if you come you can bring the lace and the chasuble too; otherwise you have done everything well.

5. May God continue his grace to you; all the good we have is God's! And ours is wretchedness and nothing else.4

Goodbye; more in person your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Cf. L 320.

2 Cf. L 320,3; 322.

3 She does not finish the sentence; perhaps she meant that she needed money.

4 The call to humility was needed so that Sr. A. Veneranda could face the difficulties peacefully and without alarm.

She should be more careful to forestall the Sisters' mistakes. She asks her to collect a Sister's money, sending her the power of attorney.

A.M.F. Dear daughter,

1. As for the teachers, I tell you it all depended on you; you should never have allowed them to go to the parlour together, alone. What do you think? Oh! poor judgement!1 So let it not happen again. Otherwise all is well, but I wish you were more watchful.

2. Here I am sending you this power of attorney and you will see. Go to this lady; she will tell you everything;2 see whether you can collect this money, which meanwhile will serve to send something to those sisters. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The two Sisters, present in the parlour when the girls' parents visited,

had advised the girls to buy sweets and mints instead of handing the money received to the Superior to keep for their necessary expenses.

2 The power of attorney. A lady in Florence wanted Sr. A. Riparata Fabrini to collect the sum in her savings book. Cf. L 1.7.1879 to M. Rosa.

She expects her in Piacenza by the 20th of the month, together with the Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received yours;1 of course I shall do as you thought;2 hurry, come, come; I expect you by the 20th. Oh! as soon as the examinations are over leave with Sr. A.;3 I have already written to the Superior. Come; everything in person. Greetings to the sisters, and I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The Sister wrote on 3 July: the pupils' examinations will begin on the 8th and end on 13 July.

2 The Mayor has learned of her transfer and opposes it. It is better not to tell him until after she has left. So Sr. A. Agnese to the

Mother.

3 Leave with Sr. A. Fabia. Cf. L 344,2.

She thanks her and says she has sent the cloth.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received the cheese, a thousand thanks; I enclose the letter for the Canon, but will he do it?2 Enough, I leave it to the Lord.

2. I am sending you the scotch cloth, but you don't tell me the quantity or quality; I fear I may get it wrong! Enough, I am in an abyss of business. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the L of 7.7.1879 to which the Mother replies.

2 She had told her of Canon Biagini's intentions regarding the will. Cf. L 326, n. 3. She encloses a letter for him, as Sr.

A. Crocifissa had suggested.

She was wrong to approach the Mayor; she should be patient and let the Mother write.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You made a great mess by writing that letter,1

while I was acting with the other one; enough. Be patient and do not move a piece, for I am doing enough from here and I hope it will all end soon; otherwise they will certainly not be very pleas-

2. Now, a day earlier or a day later should not

trouble you so much, when you know for certain that I am pressing hard from here.3 Everything in person, but be calm, for pity's sake. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Having received the Mother's invitation to come to Piacenza, Sr. A. Agnese, in agreement with the Superior, had forwarded to the Mayor notice of the

"General's" order to leave by the 20th. She felt bound to obey and so asked him to arrange for the examinations to be finished by that date.

2 The Mother disapproves of the move; she is dealing with it personally; she hopes the matter can be settled without upsetting the local authorities.

3 I am pressing hard: I insist.

She expects her with the girls. She answers some questions and advises her what to do.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter Benedetta,

1. It seems a thousand years to you because I do not write.1 Oh! if you could see me! Yesterday I had a very bad headache; today I am free of it, but there is so much to do you would not believe it!

2. So on Saturday without fail you will be here, won't you? with the girls. I telegraphed you and now I am answering the other letter.

3. As for the alms-collectors: poor creatures, they go round and then they will pay as they always have, since that bad one had let everything go to ruin.2

4. So find out a little about the examinations; otherwise bring Sr. A. Fulvia here with you, so she can resit her subject; and that muddler from Ferrara you say is good for nothing, better tell her so and send her home; bring her, and I shall have her accompanied at once; meanwhile in the holidays she is no use at all, none; bring her.3

5. More in person, dear Benedetta; think of one thing only: that your poor Mother is yours alone, and will be for eternity.

Affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Benedetta had written to her on 8 July.

2 As for... ruin. Regarding the alms-collecting Sisters she confirms what

Benedetta had written. It is true, they get tired and then they will pay the debts as usual, while the Superior has run up debts and proved incompetent.

3 That muddler you mention is the young teacher from Ferrara, whom

Benedetta described thus: "she knows nothing except how to dirty exercise books."

At last she has received a letter. She will try to prepare the ten Sisters Father Rocchi is coming to collect. She should try to have the journey paid for, as is done for other Sisters. She is in deficit from the expense of the first expedition. The Bishop should apply to the Bishop of Piacenza for information on the Institute. Various suggestions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. At last, after so long, at last I receive a letter from you,1 for

I had received none for two months. I assure you

I felt indescribable pain, my God! For pity's sake, write to me!

I see that a whole regiment of my letters has gone astray; you ask why; this letter of yours is dated 15 May; just imagine, I received it on 10 July.2 You see, my dear!

2. In it you tell me that Father Rocchi will come to fetch ten sisters and that I should see they are of good will.3 Dear daughter, I shall do all I can, but it depends on their good will and on praying the Lord to preserve our vocation;

otherwise, patience is needed.

3. The scotch cloth was sent at once, and I even added the tibet for the scapulars.4

4. I hope I shall be well off regarding the others who are to go;5 I would suggest you think of getting me something for the journey, because the cost of such expeditions is too much for me. I have not yet recovered from yours. You should know that the

Sisters of Charity receive 1000 francs each6 for the small expenses of their journey. What do you think? Certainly their house gains by it and they do not have deficits as I do. Certainly in this way one can never have anything. I leave it to your heart to imagine my position, which is truly painful.7 So, my dear daughter, I urge this on you warmly.

5. As for the Bishop, you must stand firm and reply that if he has anything to say he should apply to the Bishop of Piacenza, who is the Protector, and likewise to the Mother; the Sacred Congregation knows nothing of it, because it will do nothing but apply to the Bishop of the diocese where the mother house now is, and he is the Protector; so he should take care to send his letters to him, in order to get better and fairer replies.8

6. As for the Confessor, let the Sisters go to the extraordinary confessor as often as they wish. I hear they like this, so try to satisfy them. Father Rocchi cannot take it amiss, since he is his Superior, can he? So that is how it is put right.

7. Take care of yourself. I hear you already have a new sister and I am very glad.9 I wish you would make many, so that you can send them or bring them to me. Oh! if only that moment would really come!10 So write to me a lot and tell me many things.

[Your affectionate M. ROSA]

1 It is dated 15 May 1879.

2 You ask why: yours, to which I am replying, is of 15 May; she received it on 10 July. The post takes months to arrive. But the

Sister had written other letters earlier. Cf. L 342,1.

3 She asked for 10 Sisters: a teacher, a piano teacher and others as nurses, since the hospitals were large, with 220-240 patients.

4 Cf. L 299, n. 11; 328, n. 2.

5 I hope I shall get some help with the journey of the Sisters who are to go.

6 Caduna: each.

7 Cf. L 311,5; 328,4.

8 The Bishop of La Paz wants to know the amount of the dowry required to enter the Institute.

9 There is a young woman asking to receive the FSA habit.

10 "There are many postulants who want to enter", Sr. A.

Giuseppa reported.

The Sisters are granted renewal of vows, and first profession is granted to those who have completed a year since clothing, subject to the Superiors' approval.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Permission is given to renew the Holy Vows1 to all the sisters who made them last year, provided the Superior has no observation to make. If she has anything to say, let her do so at once.

2. Likewise permission is given to make the Holy Vows to those who have completed the year since clothing, and for these too the Superior must scrupulously report if she does not find them worthy.

3. The Holy Vows are not permitted to those who have not completed the year since clothing, even if they ask.

May the Lord bless you!

[Your affectionate M. ROSA]

1 Professions are generally made on the feast of Saint Anne, 26 July.

She has received other letters, but not the one with the accounts. She hopes hers has arrived. Encouragement and news. The novena of Saint Anne begins; she is sure they too will hold a fine celebration in her honour.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have just received three letters: two from you and one entirely from the sisters. In your two there were also some from the sisters, one dated 2 May and the other the 6th of the same month. You say you wrote me one on 27 April telling me about the accounts and your balance sheet, but I did not receive it.1 Oh! how distressing! It is better not to write certain things, you understand? For pity's sake, I urge you! My God, what if it fell into their hands?2

2. I hear you say the Sisters are not behaving very well. My God, what pain this is for me! Take courage, and first use every gentle means and then firm ones; I am very grieved, and I assure you I do nothing but pray for you.

3. I also hear you hope the benefactor will buy you a house.3 Oh! what a comfort; at least you will no longer have to fear being sent away.

4. I hope you have received my letter telling you about the Protector, and many things that will have pleased you.4 I am sending you this one; tell the Sisters I have already written to them and will answer these at once too, but I am so busy that I really don't know how to manage! I won't speak of my health, for it is always very poor, but I am always on my feet, and there is so much [work]. My God, when I think of the letter that was lost, it occurs to me that it may be the one you say went round the whole city and then you don't know where it ended up. Ah! how distressing! see if you can find out anything.

5. Tomorrow the Saint's novena begins; if you could see how beautifully we have prepared it!5 How many gifts she has received! Oh! what consolation6 (if she could have it) our Dear Holy Mother would have, wouldn't she? Surely you too will hold a fine celebration, won't you? Oh! Yes, I don't doubt it.

6. For pity's sake, take care of yourself and don't be upset, for these are small things and Jesus puts everything right; I hope so!

Greetings to all the Sisters; I wish them a thousand blessings from Heaven, and I remain for ever

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 None of these three letters has survived.

2 Into the hands of the administrators there.

3 The benefactor is Benigno Clavijo.

4 It is L 340. The Protector: Bishop Mgr G. B. Scalabrini.

5 Decorated with flowers and lights.

6 How many gifts: ex-votos in thanksgiving and homage; what consolation she would have if she could have them there too.

Words of comfort.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. A line of comfort; and if I could, I would tell you so many things; I only assure you that I share your sorrows and, clinging to my Crucified,2

Affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the correspondence between the Sister and the Mother.

2 The Mother, herself ill, comforts her Crocifissa, who had confessed her state of "deep dejection". Cf. her L dated 18.7.1879.

She must be in Piacenza on the 29th with Sr. A. Fabia, who has examinations to sit. She should do her best to bring forward the pupils' final examinations. Advice and good wishes for the feast of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A hasty line; listen carefully. Tell the Superior I have received her registered letter and thank her; I shall write to her another time.1

2. You must come together with Sr. A. Fabia, but you should make it known that she must be here by the 29th, because on 4 August she has to be in Crema for her examinations.2 So you must be here on the 29th. Beg them to let you hold the examinations on the 28th, so that you have a companion for the journey. If they refuse me this, they are certainly doing it on purpose! Oh! God! how distressing; do not leave without holding the examinations.3 Patience is needed! Ah! whoever gets involved... Be calm, for I take your part entirely and share your disappointment.4

3. As for the postulants, let us say no more; I will not accept the last one.5 Now I think I have made myself clear; tell the Superior that, regarding the matters she mentions, she should hand everything to you and send me nothing more.6

4. Have a fine feast, be joyful; I wish it you, as I wish you a thousand blessings, and I am

Your affectionate M. ROSA

Have the Superior read this letter of mine, and understand it well.

1 The Superior Sr. A. Genoveffa Molinari.

2 Sr. A. Fabia had to sit the examinations for her teaching certificate.

3 The examinations were not brought forward; they were held in the first ten days of August.

4 Sr. A. Agnese wanted to leave at once.

5 Two postulants had come forward. One had then withdrawn; the other seemed very undecided.

6 The money she had collected from the Town Council as arrears of salary.

She has been ill in bed. She is praying for the examinations. She expects her in Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Courage; if I have not written it is because I was in bed; today I am barely up. In person we shall tell each other many things.1

2. I shall not stop praying; your examinations, you will see, will go wonderfully and you will be pleased.2 Tell me, whom will you leave in your place when you come? See that no fewer than 3 or 4 sisters remain. Goodbye your affectionate M. ROSA

Sr. A. Celsa was to go to Piacenza for the spiritual exercises. The pupils' examinations at the end of the school year.

Transfers of Sisters. For a sick one she thinks it best to go to Spello, as she cannot take her in at Piacenza. She leaves her free to decide about other sisters and admission to vows.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. Barely up, I write to you in my own hand to tell you several little things. Listen, Sr. A. Beniamina1 will be sent back to you from Gualdo, for it has been discovered that this sister has always written secretly to

Appignano; she did the same when she was there; keep a close watch on her.

2. The other is Sr. A. Celeste,2 I don't know, the one who went to

Appignano ill and they don't want her there. Very well, you could see about taking her to Spello for the air; the doctor says that if she has a change of air she will soon recover. Try it; otherwise send her to me.

3. I would take them all, but here for the moment I cannot, because I have had trouble over this.3 It is a small town and we do not want it thought that those who die are not of this house but of others.4

4. Listen, I would signo (?) this plan to the Spello hospital: that I shall pay for this sister to stay there; what do you say?

5. Listen, for the Saint's feast the two from S. Martinello will come to you; as their superior is coming there, they are left alone.5 What do you say? You could give them one to keep them company until the superior goes back, if you think fit.6

6. I leave you free to do what seems best. Likewise for the vows: let only those make or renew them whom you consider worthy and who will not trample on them; act yourself, and you can use the words: the mother does not permit it.7 How is the Bishop?8

Goodbye, yours for ever

Affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Beniamina Baraldi had been at Gualdo Tadino only a short time. Cf. L

324,1.

2 Sr. A. Celeste Locci.

3 In Piacenza, a small town, people were surprised that so many Sisters died.

4 The Mother withdrew sick Sisters from other houses and had them treated in

Piacenza in the infirmary set up for the purpose in Via della Morte.

5 For the feast of Saint Anne the Superior and one of the Sisters of

S. Martinello would go to Foligno.

6 If she thinks fit, she can send someone to keep the Sisters left there company.

7 and you can use the expression: the mother does not permit it.

8 The Bishop of Foligno, Mgr Nicola Grispignani, who was ill, was being nursed by the Sisters. Cf. L 351,5 and n. 4.

She is unwell. She wishes them a happy feast of Saint Anne and gives her blessing.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just one line, because I am barely up and unwell. Be of good heart; celebrate your feast joyfully and happily; renew your Vows.1 In short, I wish you a thousand blessings from Heaven, and believe me always

affectionate M. ROSA

Greetings to all.

1 The four Sisters of the community were all in temporary vows.

Praise and encouragement. She is glad the Sisters are going to celebrate Saint Anne with those of the Genoa community, and that these will visit her the next day.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your two lines; well done, courage! The answers you gave to ... were inspired by God.1

2. Listen, you will have received yours in which I told you to go on the Saint's day and that the next day those from Genoa should come to you. If Fr Accinelli will not come, find a priest to say Holy Mass for you, and do everything prudently; I urge you strongly to act prudently.2

3. I have written to Sr. A. Illuminata to wait for the teacher.3 Write to me often. See that the girls are well dressed and clean for Saturday in Genoa.4

Goodbye; I am so unwell that writing is an effort. Sure that all will go well, goodbye, yours for ever affectionate M. ROSA

1 The letter referred to is missing, so it is impossible to understand.

2 Everything prudently, to avoid friction and misunderstandings.

3 Sr. A. Illuminata Cavassa, superior of the community in Rome, Vicolo

Margana, was temporarily at Sestri P.

4 On Saturday, the feast of Saint Anne, they would go to Genoa, to the community of nursing Sisters.

She thanks her for the lace and the prayers. She should do as she thinks best about the postulant.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A thousand thanks for the lovely lace and for all the prayers you say for me. If I do not write at length you will understand why: it is two days before the feast;1 just imagine!...

2. As for the postulant, I leave you free to do as you think best.2

3. Have a good feast and make your Vows,3 and believe me yours; a thousand blessings from heaven, and I am yours, all of you, for ever

affectionate M. ROSA

1 of the feast of Saint Anne.

2 A young woman wishing to join the FSA had come forward.

3 Cf. L 327,4.

She urges her to accept nursing the sick and to give good example. She should send the transferred Sister's linen at once.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I urge you, if sick people come, to accept them and never let it appear that we do it for gain, as that wretched woman did!1 Oh! What stabs these are, my daughter!2 If you only knew!

2. Enough; please send me all her things at once, but not the little boots she said they should send, nor3 the new apron; not the black clothes; all the linen. At once, I beg you.

Goodbye, I am your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 ...never let it appear. Not to give the impression that we care for the sick for gain, as did the Sister she had to transfer.

Wretched, because she dishonoured the Institute by violating one of the most important points of the Rule: free care of the sick.

2 Stabs: wounds caused by the seriousness of the breach.

3 nemo: not even.

She concerns herself with some sisters who need sea bathing.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. My God! I would like to have all, all the sick with me, but if I said I did not know where to send the one with the bad knee for sea bathing, it is because the two houses we have by the sea are full of sisters whom the doctors are now sending for sea baths; yet I see none of them comes out cured.1

2. Enough; send the sister to Sestri and she will be received. I shall take one away at once and you can send the other, yours, there.

3. As for the journey I don't know what to say; you would have to have her accompanied, going by way of Pisa: Florence-Pisa and Genoa-Sestri.

4. Enough, do what you think best; if you think of sending Sr. A. Margherita too, for it does her fevers much good and she will recover sooner, I leave it to you to do what is best.2

5. Today I am writing to the duchess,3 but I have such a headache that I really have to force myself to write. You did well to take the coffee. Greetings to all and to the Bishop;4 a blessing for me your affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. Let those from S. Martinello go alone. They will soon have their new Superior.5

Goodbye, yours

1 None comes out: comes out cured.

2 Sr. A. Margherita could accompany her; the change of air would do her good.

3 Cf. L 128, n. 1. Duchess Agnese Boncompagni.

4 She had nursed the sick Bishop during the night. At three o'clock he had celebrated Mass in his room and then offered the two Sisters coffee. Cf.

L 346,6 and n. 8.

5 Cf. L 346,5. She would send a new Superior.

She has sent her a sack of maize. The tenant farmer should trust the new landlord. If she thinks fit, she can go to Sestri to greet him.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

1. Your long letter was dear to me, though I have such a headache that writing is an effort. Oh! that unhappy woman has done all sorts of things!1 Let us pray for her.

2. Tell me, have you received the sack of maize? Ask at the station, it will be there; since the miller sent it, I cannot send you the receipt, but as soon as he comes I shall get it from him.

3. Courage; tell the manente2 not to worry, that he is dealing with a fine, good landlord and will be able to obtain everything, and he can be sure of it.3 They are at Sestri taking the sea baths; they left last night; if you want to see them, tell him to go too and he will see that he gets everything. Goodbye. May the Lord send you his providence. Goodbye. The Lady cannot be accepted,4 you understand, don't you?

Goodbye, yours for ever affectionate M. ROSA

1 Cf. L 350.

2 The manente, in Genoese dialect: the tenant farmer.

3 ...fine, good landlord: Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei, husband of

Carlotta. The Mother had appointed him her general attorney in January 1877.

4 She wanted to join the FSA.

She has received her letter, which comforted her. She encourages her. Always and everything for Jesus.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. A line in the greatest haste and with a headache. Your long letter was a real comfort to me.1

2. Courage, and always everything for Jesus, for his glory, always, always.2 Goodbye. Greetings to you all, and may God bless you all.

I am for ever

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 A real comfort because of the excellent results of the girls' examinations before a board of twelve examiners.

2 In the same letter of 29 July 1879 she had told her of the feast of

Saint Anne and of the Sisters' and her own deep joy at the renewal of religious vows.

She asks for news.

A.M.F.

1. I want to know whether you ate with appetite, whether you would like an egg. How are you? I want to know what you would like.2

Goodbye; get well soon, do you understand?3 I cannot manage the stairs; see you tomorrow

[affectionate Mother]

1 The date is inferred from the context. The Sister, having left Bovino on 10 August, had gone to Piacenza. After a period of rest the Mother intended to send her to Ferrara as superior and head of the school.

2 The Mother herself looks after her.

3 A very demanding task of considerable

responsibility awaited her in Ferrara.

She suggests to her dear niece how to answer her father, who is unhappy with her choice of life. Encouragement and greetings.

A.M.F

My daughter,

1. I am answering yours at once, so that you can answer Papa1 like this:

2. "Yes, dear Papa, I do not want to hear of marriage; this is my state of life and I cannot hear of any other. Dear Papa, I know well too that, if it was a brilliant match, it was also difficult, because it concerned... and the rest you can learn from your aunt.2 Were he a prince and nothing stood in the way, I would still remain firm in this state. I am happy and hope to be so all my life".3

3. And then thank him; but write at once. When I come, you will hear. Pray that I may come soon, though it certainly won't be before Monday.4

4. Take courage, for the devil will lose.

5. Tell them all that I am sorrier than they are that we cannot be together, but the days, so many things, and you will hear.5

Goodbye, I really have no time your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Her father, Angelo Savignone, disapproved of his daughter's choice; he would have preferred the good match in view to come off.

2 ...if it was brilliant, it concerned ...aunt. There was evidently some impediment of a moral or religious nature. The aunt: M. Rosa.

3 In any case her choice could not be measured by standards of human greatness and power.

4 Monday the 18th. Nothing is known of her going to Sestri.

5 Tell them all, Benedetta, Carla, Gaspare, that I am sorrier than they are... but the days pass, so many things happen, you will hear everything.

She urges thrift, obedience and observance. Better to die than to stray.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received the little box with the picture, and one thing pleased me, the picture, but not the sweets, because that is money wasted and I do not think it right to act like this.1

2. So never do it again, because if you saw how many Sisters we are and what it takes to support them! My God!

3. As for what you tell me about obedience, you are to obey no one but me and our Father, and the Bishop;2 and I tell you that as for the rest, I tell you it is better to lose everything rather than break a Rule.3

4. So be strong, daughter; let everything be done without human respect, and think only of being observant if you want to please God and be a true Daughter of Saint Anne. Do you understand? Better to die than to stray. So stand firm until death. Whoever perseveres is sure of eternal life.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 She had sent her an embroidered picture and a box of Sicilian sweets. As for the latter, the Mother points out that it was an unnecessary expense. Economy is necessary, because there are so many Sisters and much money is needed to support them.

2 About obedience. On 16 August the Superior had written to her that the

"delegated canon" was imposing "rules his own way" without regard for our rules, and she had had to appeal to the Bishop for permission to go to Palermo. The Mother answers clearly: obey her and our Father (Tornatore), and the Bishop in matters concerning the running of the work.

3 One of the proposals contrary to the Rule: during the holidays, admitting outside young ladies to table with the Sisters. Cf. L G. Martinelli to M. Rosa, 7.8.1879.

She receives no letters or news and is very anxious. In Italy there are many requests for Daughters of Saint Anne; in Sicily 6 houses have opened and requests for Sisters are pending for as many more. Providence is not lacking, but expenses are great, food is dear, there is poverty and people are suffering. She gives news of Canon Biagini of Pistoia. She begs her to write and not keep her longing any more.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. How sad not to receive letters from you! What are you doing? Not even a line in those from the sisters; and I cannot understand how you have not yet received the scotch cloth and all the accounts with the receipt for tracing it.2 My God! What a distance! Truly a very great sorrow!

2. I have written to the Bishop, to Father Rocchi and to the Nuncio, and no reply ever comes; I thought I would hear of the Father's arrival here in Piacenza to fetch the others, but all my hopes have vanished.3

3. Dear daughter, the requests we have here in Italy for Daughters of Saint Anne are a great matter. There is Sicily, which would like a million of them, and I assure you I don't know how [to manage]. We already have 6 houses there, but they are asking for as many more. Soon we shall be in all the main cities of Sicily, not counting those opening and the requests4 we have here. I don't know how to meet them all.

4. Oh! how good the Lord is, who provides so well for his poor daughters! All I lack is a little money to do what is still needed, because, (as); if you knew what a burden the rent of the Rome house is!5

5. Oh! here this year food is unbelievably dear, and I assure you it is a worry that pains me greatly, with so many people. The harvest has been small and poor everywhere. Oh, what poverty one sees! My dear, if you were here you would say: "Oh! how sad!"6 So remember one who suffers and groans under so dreadful a burden, and that there are still many bills to pay.7

6. You will be curious to hear the news from Pistoia: things are just as you left them; the shouting goes on, and worse; I assure you it is a real s[candal].8 Ah! how painful it is to see and hear certain things! Pray and have others pray that God may lay his holy hand on it, so that before they die both may be converted, for it is a serious matter.

7. Give the sisters my love and tell them to write to me, for their letters are very dear to me; likewise yours and Father Rocchi's, who never writes. As for you, I am really sorry, because it is clear you let the packets9 go without writing and go months without a sign of life. Well done! You have done as the proverb says, "out of sight, out of mind"; that is what you do. Thank you!10

8. It is not like that with me; even when I am ill in bed I keep lamenting: "but why don't they write? What are they doing? And Sr. A. Giuseppa? Oh, why keep me longing so!!"

9. Greet all the sisters and Father Rocchi for me, and the postulants if you have any. Please write to me more often; otherwise it is a real ordeal.

Goodbye; may the Lord bless you and all the sisters, and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

My daughter,

C.3 could tell you what sincere and true affection I bear you, my dear; so remember I am always close to you; you say you have so much to tell me, and I?! Ah! It is immense!

your affectionate M. ROSA

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. In haste. Note: the money I sent you is for Masses, at one and a half francs each;1 those I sent you are at one and a half francs, and when I have had them said I need the celebrant's receipt stating that he has said them.2

2. Listen, I am sending you a folded sheet already started, so the Priest can sign it each time he celebrates, and when there are 20 you will send me the sheet and I shall send you one and a half francs per Mass.3 Do you understand?

3. You say you will engage the Chaplain;4 tell him yes; I guarantee him a Mass every day at one franc a Mass, and now I have 60 at one and a half francs; if he wants all 60, let him write to me; but here I think I am telling you plainly: let him celebrate 17 Masses and then send me a receipt, as I too must give one. I see it is done everywhere; he need only mark the number of Masses and his name.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. How sad never to have letters from you: for a month and a half I have known nothing! For pity's sake, do not let the mail packets go without writing to me; it is true I did the same this month, but in other months I never let one go.1

2. You will understand the reason for this negligence of mine: it came from the immense amount of business, which, I assure you, even sapped my strength. Although I did not call the Superiors together this year,2 there has still been plenty of work, and there still is.

3. I am partly up and partly in bed, for my health keeps declining and the swelling is getting worse.3 Enough, I leave to God the care of this wretched pig, which truly disgusts me, to think that a God so infinitely powerful and supreme should stoop to sustain so abject a creature, loathsome in every respect.4

4. Oh! how great is the goodness of the Heart of Jesus!! Yes! I am overwhelmed merely thinking of it and cannot help exclaiming constantly: "Oh goodness beyond compare!"5

5. How much money and trouble it took to send you those things for you! It is a big case, and you will see (if it arrives safely) that you will be pleased. They would not accept the soap,6 but my brothers told me they would get it to you all the same. If you would like to apply to them directly, as they trade with Buenos Aires, I am sending you the address [of] Federico Gattorno.7

6. Now I inform you that the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and

Regulars has approved and given permission to hold Clothings of Daughters of Saint Anne there in La Paz too, and will already have sent a letter to the Apostolic Delegate there; perhaps he has already told you.

7. I should really like to know whether it is worthwhile sending another 10 sisters and whether the house can gain something from it; so you must tell me frankly how things stand,8 because I would prepare a good [number]; but on the other hand, having so many fine houses to open here, I do not think it right to do so much for one place when, the year is now far gone, and I cannot say I have even a likelihood of any benefit.9 What do you say?

8. Listen, when you write, explain yourself a little better, because your letters are so concise that I understand little or nothing. So write more often and in more detail. I am anxious when a month passes without news.

9. This time I am not writing to Father Rocchi, because I have already written to him twice and he has never answered what I asked. So for 10 sisters, besides the journey, he must also give me a premium10 to provide their trousseau.

10. Greetings to all; I wish you a thousand blessings from heaven, while I remain for ever your

affectionate M. ROSA

My daughter,

1. I hear of your distress and am very, very grieved,1 because they have offended the heart of Jesus with their hellish gossip. Read them these two lines of mine!

2. Daughters, how can you have listened so much to the devil, letting yourselves be seduced into ugly, wretched thoughts against your Superior? while I wish you a thousand blessings from Heaven, and may they make you live as true Daughters of Saint Anne, and I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She copies for her the letters sent to the Bishop and the Nuncio in La Paz, containing the rules on the local Superior's duties and on the Novitiate to be set up in La Paz. She urges observance and the formation of the Sisters. She waits in vain for news.

A.M.F.

Dearest Daughter,

1. I am sending you a copy of what I wrote to the Bishop and the Nuncio, which is what1 the S. C. of Bishops and Regulars [has laid down], and so you are to arrange things as I tell you below; and you will appoint Sr. A. Livia as mistress.2 Here is what I tell you:

Most Reverend Excellency, I am replying to Your Excellency's esteemed letter of 20 July. Here is what pertains to the Superior.

She has all her authority from the Mother General. She has no fixed term of office, but the General can remove her at any time she sees fit - this is not contrary to the agreement made with your Republic to leave the sisters sent there for 10 years, since that does not concern offices.3 As regards these, the Mother General is free to change them -.

Her purpose is to safeguard observance of the Rule in the community entrusted to her by the Mother General.4 She therefore has authority to admonish anyone who fails in observance and to impose a penance proportioned to the fault; if the offender persists, she reports it to the General.5

She has authority to assign the sisters to the various duties of the Family, except that of portress, who is appointed directly by the General.

She has no power either to change or to add anything to the daily timetable and customs of the Institute without the express permission of the General.

I also think it my duty to inform Your Excellency that the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars has granted me the faculty to establish a novitiate there, in agreement with the Apostolic Delegate of your Republic.

I outline the rules of that Novitiate.

1st Postulants will spend two months on trial before receiving the habit.

2nd After receiving the habit they will spend six months there.

3rd After six months in the habit there,6 they must come to complete the other six months of novitiate here in Italy at the Mother House in Piacenza. The journey is to be at the Novice's expense.

4th The dowry must be such as corresponds here in Italy to One Thousand Lire (1000). The Novice Mistress is appointed by the Mother General; she is to instruct the Novices well in the Rule and customs. Therefore, as far as possible, the Novices will not be employed in nursing the sick, but will attend only to cleansing themselves of faults brought from the world and putting on the spirit of the Institute. The age for acceptance must be from fifteen to twenty-five. If older, she is not to be accepted without first consulting the General. Your Excellency asks what the means of support are. The means of support recognised by Rome are these:7 1st The Mother House has property.8 2nd No Houses are founded unless there are funds, or a per capita allowance sufficient for food and clothing. 3rd Superiors are obliged to send all surpluses to the Mother House.9

2. I cannot understand why I never receive letters from you. If you wrote to me twice a month I should receive them; I want you to do so, and so have more detailed news from there;10 in your last you led me to hope that Father Rocchi would come again to fetch the sisters; I have them ready, but, as I told you, it must not happen again that I have to provide their trousseau.

3. Oh! Dear daughter! you will surely not believe how distressed I am. Moreover there is still the whole case of goods I sent you, which adds up to a fine bill that I shall soon have sent to you, but the merchant will not hear of waiting.11

4. I urge observance on you, and I would like the sisters to go to the church for their prayers and meditation.

5. Daughter, if you do not attend to works of piety, your community will be lost. Oh! whoever lives distracted is soon lost, especially a sister always immersed in worldly things; if she does not take care to recollect herself in God, a bad end soon comes!

6. And if a superior does not take good care that her subjects are observant, alas! what becomes of them!

7. So you can allow them to go to the extraordinary confessor more often; in short, everything lies in knowing how to cultivate them. They are plants that wither without fertiliser, and we must water them with the life-giving water our master Jesus spoke of to the Samaritan woman.

8. So a Superior must do everything so that her sisters may drink their fill of that water: meditation done well in church, prayers likewise in church; and she should gather them often and give them fine exhortations.

9. Do not allow them to converse with lay people, especially when these are sick, but let them keep well away from conversing with lay people; and the superior should, as far as she can, be among them, or else someone acting for her.

10. If you knew how constantly I think of these blessed creatures! You surely won't believe it; from morning till night I think of you, and when a month has passed without news of you the thought truly afflicts me.

11. I keep saying that my Giuseppa is doing as the proverb says: "out of sight, out of mind."12 For pity's sake, observance of the Holy Rules! So write to me, a lot, and something comforting, for I have more than enough bitter things.

12. Give my warm greetings to Father Rocchi; tell him I am waiting for him to come and bring me some first fruits from America, that is, a Novice, at least one, whom I shall hold dear.

Goodbye to all; may the Lord bless you, and believe me always

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 which is what: that is, the instructions of the S. C. of Bishops and Regulars.

2 Novice Mistress will be Sr. A. Livia Tallarini.

3 The Sisters' duties.

4 The Superior's main purpose is to safeguard observance of the Rule in the community entrusted to her by the Mother General.

5 ... penance... offender... reports: to give anyone who has broken the rule the salutary punishment for amendment; in case of obstinacy and insubordination, she should report the case to the General.

6 Six months from clothing.

7 Rome: the ecclesiastical authorities in Rome, that is, the S. C. of BB. and RR.

8 It has its own property.

9 They are obliged because the religious Family has a centralised administration and must ensure fair sharing and support for members and works.

10 Cf. L 369,1.

11 Cf. L 369,5, 7 and 9.

12 Cf. L 357,7.

She has received three letters. Sorry about her illness, she urges her to take care. Advice and warnings about observance. She approves the opening of the school and the management of the hospital. She is pleased that a young American has received the habit.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Oh! how comforting to read your three letters, which I receive all together, registered, along with the sisters'; - I don't know how to send this great packet of letters all together registered - two dated 14 September and one dated 8 August, and likewise the sisters'.

2. Enough, now let us come to you.2 I kept saying: "Alas! my Giuseppa is certainly ill, for otherwise she would surely write to me". The sisters too, not writing me even a line; what ugly behaviour!

3. For pity's sake, take care of yourself; I want to hear you are always well. I hear too that the sisters have been ill. Let us hope that now, being more acclimatised, you will not have to suffer so much.3

4. I am truly sorry to hear how badly the sisters are behaving regarding obedience and the confessor; they do little honour to one who bears the name of Daughter of Saint Anne, who lives only by obedience and even breathes by pure obedience.4 These, whom I thought had no will of their own any more, but were always intent on their sanctification and on giving an extraordinary example, such as to draw from everyone in La Paz: "Oh! they are Angels!

5. You, my dear, allow me to tell you one thing: take great care never to speak alone with outsiders, so that the sisters are not scandalised; rather tell the listening sister frankly: "withdraw a moment - but always where you can be seen - and I do this with my Superiors' permission"; and when you write, mention the times you have had to do so out of necessity. Oh! If only you knew how to value this observance of yours! I beg you to put it into practice.5

6. For the rest, I am comforted and congratulate you on opening the new House, and I rejoice greatly. Send for the Sisters, but give me two months' notice.6

7. Listen, Father Rocchi need not come to fetch them; they could come by themselves; just send me the exact itinerary of the journey you made. I am sure they would be better off; only I would like them to give me not only the travel costs but also money for the trousseau, as it is too great an expense,7 and the money Father Rocchi would spend on his own journey there and back would go to the sisters, wouldn't it?

8. Now let us turn to the hospital. I leave it to you to take over full management, and it will be this: put down the money you are to receive; you will not have to deal with land or anything else, but you will be given a sum and you must provide for everything. Is that it? Because if it were otherwise I would not think it feasible.8

9. I am sending you another sheet about the bull, and the rest I have sent to the Bishop, so you will have it by now too.9 I am sending you the paper for collecting the scotch cloth; try to pay for it if you can, because I am really burdened. Oh! what a year for us! it is dreadful! a general famine; if you saw it, it is truly pitiful!10

Remember it is Jesus, whether one or another!12

Mother, and if she gives you her permission I am ready to do what she tells me". Meanwhile be firm; keep a close eye on those you mention, with regard to the praticanti;13 they frighten me. Otherwise, why do you tell me not to scold you?14 Oh! daughter, why are you afraid? No, no, be of good heart and believe me always, for ever and ever, amen

She asks him to intervene to clarify the Parish Priest's position on the Infant School and to state the Administration's intentions about whether the Sisters should stay.

[Dear Mr Mayor,]

1. I very much regret having to trouble you to obtain from

Your Most Illustrious Lordship clarification and also justice concerning what I am about to relate about a letter just received from the Very Rev. Parish Priest of your town.1

2. He complains of the Superior and wishes her to be removed. I would not be unwilling to do this, adding this sacrifice to the many I have already made for that infant school, without any complaint on my part, as for example having had to recall the sisters several times this winter, now for a change of air to restore their health, now to exchange them for others, now to change the Superior at the instigation2 of the Rev. Parish Priest, who no longer wanted her.

3. Of the present Superior,3 whom he also wants removed, the said Parish Priest writes precisely this in his letter: "I have heard complaints from the Administration, which, having to provide furniture and linen4 for the Infant School in question, which lacks them, is under no obligation to do so except for three sisters, not four, and this is also noticed by the townspeople, much stirred up by troublemakers"; and he concludes that it is absolutely necessary to remove the Superior and leave her duties to one of the sisters, so that only three sisters remain.

4. Not long ago I informed Your Lordship that it was impossible to leave only three Sisters there; and the Infant School Administration agreed that I should replace the Superior with another, as I did, and that there should be four sisters, not three.

5. Now, if desired, I shall also change the present Superior and put in another, though I am surprised that this should burden the Administration as regards furniture and linen. There are four beds, which are just enough for the four sisters. As for linen, which would amount only to two pairs [of] sheets, two pillowcases and a few napkins and towels, it seems to me so petty an economy that I cannot believe an Administration would want to make it. However that may be, I am ready to send these things myself as soon as Your Lordship lets me know.

6. Your Lordship must also do me justice regarding a charge painful to the Institute,5 for you know it is undeserved. The Rev. Parish Priest tells me that the Superior, meddling in the Infant School's supplies, takes it upon herself to appropriate what is not hers, to the great displeasure of the members of the Infant School Administration. On this I ask for clarification and defence.

7. I can tell you, therefore, that such an affront, after so many sacrifices the Institute has borne for that Infant School, is truly undeserved, for we do not seek to profit from Infant Schools6 but to help them with collections and the like when there is need, as I would also be willing to do for yours if its finances were really exhausted, as the Rev. Parish Priest claims in his letter.

8. He adds that if I want to withdraw the sisters, I may do so.7 I cannot understand what authority or office the Rev. She may open the Novitiate. She is in favour of the Novice going to Piacenza, but leaves her to decide what is best.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

1. Last night your long letter reached me.2 Oh! how comforting to hear you are better! Oh! dear daughter! Now I order you to take care of yourself and do as little as possible; I do not want you ever to get up early in the morning, and as for food, make sure you eat what you like.3

2. Tomorrow Gaspare4 is sending you a small case of good wine; drink a little every day, and if you want anything you think may do you good, write and say so, without stinting. Do you understand?

3. Oh! How it pains me when I hear that someone

[is] ill. Oh! Then indeed I think of the distance between us.

Enough, I will not lose heart; it is mountains that never meet, but while we live, at any moment there may arise an occasion for us to see each other; moreover, with this arrangement of Novices, now one and now another, I may have the good fortune of seeing you.5

4. Now let us come to the points of your letter:

1st You ask whether I received your registered letter with all the Sisters' letters inside: yes, I received it and replied at once, telling you many things, and I sent it registered.6

2nd You tell me about a postulant who is illegitimate, whose dowry a benefactress of yours would provide. She absolutely cannot be accepted.7

3rd As for accepting them without anything, for the moment I do not think it advisable, for many reasons.8

4th I hear Father Rocchi is displeased;9 let us pray the Lord to make him understand our spirit properly, and then he will see that the Daughters of Saint Anne are not as bad as he thinks. You have done everything well; be cheerful, for all is according to God's good pleasure.

5th I hear you have met with much opposition;10 and if it is God's work, so it must be. Courage!!!

6th It is good that you neither go nor allow the sisters to go out to meals; I see you too have found out for yourself that it is not right.11

7th About the new contract I have already replied, leaving everything to your wisdom and telling you to do it as you think best.12 I shall then approve it. Do not hesitate; act frankly: in certain matters go ahead and report to me afterwards, do you understand?

8th I hear about the two cities.13 Listen, first you must settle the journey and then a sum for the trousseau, as the Sisters of Charity do. They have their journey paid and 1000 lire each for the trousseau as well. I do not say to ask 1000 lire, but at least 500 or 400. You can see the sacrifice is great, and these gentlemen save it back in the hospitals themselves.

9th As for the salary, my dear daughter, I tell you 700 a year is too little, because this year, as last year, the contracts with Sicily are 500 francs per sister, plus oil and wood, plus 200 francs for entry, with travel paid. So I would think the contract should be the same as the one made with La Paz. And for the sisters a stay of 10 years can be stated, as you have. There is a clause in the contract saying that if we cannot manage to live on the administration of the property, the municipality must provide you with the same allowance the Sisters of Charity receive in the neighbouring towns.14

10th I leave it to you, however, to do what you think best, always on condition there is a contract, of which I must have one copy, the sister who is to be Superior another, and the Municipality or Congregation, as the case may be, another. Do you think I have explained myself clearly? Act with courage; I repeat: I shall approve everything.

11th As for sending the sisters, I repeat what I told you in my other letter: I would like to send them alone, quite alone, without the company of friars or priests. So you can tell your benefactor; he will save both on sending someone and on that person's return journey. Being a large group and well recommended by the Consul, they could join those from other countries; what do you say? But you must let me know at least two months beforehand so that I can gather them all here and have them study Spanish well.15 As for what you have and would like to send me, oh! truly... I live in God and for him alone... you understand?16

5. I hope you have received a letter from Gaspare telling you what to do. Oh! what trouble it is to send you anything! Besides the expense there is the aggravation suffered by those who have to ship it.17

6. I hope you have also received my letters telling you that you may open a novitiate; tell the Novice I have received hers and will reply as soon as I have a moment, but tell her it was very dear to me.18 If she wants to come, I long to see her and hope that moment is not too far off. It would certainly be good to bring her, because then the others would be encouraged too; what do you say? You will know better than I how to handle such matters, being on the spot and already knowing their characters well; certainly one is better placed to see what is best.

7. Please write to Mgr Bishop and tell him many things, which are very dear to him, especially when he hears the reports of the new houses; I have already written to you to do so.19

Goodbye; may the Lord bless you and all, and believe me wholly yours for ever and ever affectionate M. ROSA P.S. Carlottina thanks you and sends greetings, as does the Count. Goodbye

your M. R.

2 For the rest, in short, I tell you: before and above any news of her activity and skill, her health is what matters to her. Cf. L 392, n. 3.

She sends the sacks and thanks her. She pours out her sadness, hoping to tell her everything in person, as both wish. She is unwell, as usual. She asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the sacks and thank you in advance; I am sending 4 sacks, send them back full.1 I also beg you as earnestly as I can to see that the Postulant's money is here by the 20th of this month; otherwise I shall not clothe her,2 because, oh! dear daughter! if you knew the state I am in!3

2. For pity's sake, bury these words in your heart, as I am sure you will, won't you? I have...4 Enough, in person when you come.

3. You long for it, and I certainly more than you, but there is the thought that if on earth we must live apart for Jesus, in heaven we shall rejoice for eternity!5 My God! If only I may get there! Oh! If my Beloved would accept my sufferings, perhaps my sins would be forgiven! But!

4. Today too I am writing, but always with my companion, the headache, which I assure you is no small thing!6 Yes! And yet if my Beloved accepted it, I could surely hope for mercy. But! Pray for me and have others pray.

5. Listen! If you could give me a sister, I would really need her!7 Enough, we shall talk about it in person, I hope.

Goodbye; greetings to the sisters; let them pray for me; I am yours for ever.

Affectionate M. ROSA

1 She sent them back full of potatoes and chestnuts.

2 The postulant was already in Piacenza; the money her family had promised to send was needed for the clothing, set for 30 November.

3 She was in deficit and engaged in much Institute business, with journeys and the opening of houses.

4 She does not state the great secret to be buried, but lets it be guessed: I have debts. Cf. L 328,4.

5 The thought: she lives her faith with deep openness to the hereafter.

6 She accepts it, despite the suffering: my companion.

7 Cf. L 426,1.

It is not advisable to come to Piacenza. She approves all she does.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. For pity's sake do not come, because I don't know whether I shall be here; be patient; we shall see each other before I go to Rome;1 I shall write to you and then you can come. Otherwise I approve all you are doing,2 and in haste I greet you all and am yours for ever

affectionate M. ROSA

1 To avoid the risk of a wasted journey it is better not to set out. She thinks they will see each other before she goes to Rome.

2 She was Superior of the Bellinzago House.

She returns the sacks and thanks her.

She is expecting her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the receipt for the sacks and await you eagerly.1 Oh! how touched I am to be given a share in your providence! Oh! the goodness of my God!2 Yes, dear daughter, I thank you as much as I can. Oh! what a state I am in!3 Enough, I hope to see you soon and you will hear. Goodbye.

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Cf. L 414,1.

2 Given a share: made a sharer in the providence bestowed on her by God's goodness through the alms of good people.

3 She is in poverty and must provide for everything. Cf. L 414, nn. 3-4.

She has done everything well. She should be cheerful and strong.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A hasty line: all you have done is well done.1 As for food, I want the sisters to continue, and you obey!2

2. Write to M.3 and tell him you have received nothing. Be cheerful and strong as bronze, and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

1 She had visited the Education Officer, told him about the School and invited him to visit it. He seemed satisfied. So she wrote.

2 The Sisters should go on preparing nourishing food for her, and she should obey.

3 She should write to Marquis Landi. Cf. L 407,4.

She should ask the Superior, Sr. A. Illuminata, for a Sister for the kitchen.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you need a cook; so for the moment Sr. A. Illuminata must be patient, and you get Sr. A. Carolina or another capable one, and later I shall send sisters.2 Goodbye, yours; I am in the greatest haste. Be patient; do not let Sr. A. Giacobba3 do the cooking, for pity's sake. Goodbye

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from a L of Sr. A. Illuminata Cavassa, Superior of the House in vicolo Margana. She wrote to the Mother on 22.11.1879 that Sr. A. Celsa had asked her for Sr. A. Carolina.

2 Sr. A. Carolina would stay until the replacement arrived.

3 Sr. A. Giacobba was ill.

She has received an invitation from the Parish Priest of Molochio to send Sisters for a school. She asks for authorisation and blessing and for some information about it.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. A fortnight ago I received a letter from a Parish Priest of Molochio,1 in Your Most Reverend Excellency's Diocese, who wanted the poor Daughters of Saint Anne for a school.

2. I replied that I would gladly send them, but that he should first write and tell me how they would be supported and housed.

3. So far I have had no reply. Meanwhile, as is our custom, before entering into negotiations when we are called to any city or town, we turn to the Ordinary;2 we first ask him for his permission and protection, submitting to him the proposals made to us, as in the present case.

4. I take this opportunity to ask Your Most Reverend Excellency a favour, which I am sure to obtain from the charity of so zealous a Pastor. Two Sisters of our Order are passing through Reggio, and I warmly commend them to you.

5. Please be so kind as to tell me something about Molochio,3 while I prostrate myself asking for your Pastoral Blessing, and remain, full of veneration, Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Humble Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

Molochio, in the Province of Reggio Calabria.

2 Cf. L 421,2.

3 The Archbishop replied on the 24th that the Parish Priest had not told him of his plan. He would write to him. If it went ahead, "you will have my full permission and they will be lovingly protected." AFSA, CvIM, 60.

She reminds her that she gave her a document as a model for a contract to be drawn up with Canon Biagini. She should search further and send it.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. How it pains me when you write that you do not have the contract!1 Alas! Dear daughter! Don't you remember that I, to show it to the Canon, told you to keep it safe in your hands, that it was Signora Maddalena Parmigiani's, don't you remember? It was to show the Canon how she had done it,2 but you were to keep it with you and give it to no one. So what is to be done? Oh! if it has been lost! Dear daughter, now I need it. Don't you remember I told you: "keep it with you and only show it?" I think it had a green or yellow band!3

2. For pity's sake, look and see whether you can find it.4 I want to hope you did not give it to the Canon and that he has not torn it up.

A thousand things are going through my mind. Write to me at once and tell me whether you have found it; secure it well under 5 seals so that it is not lost; secure it well. Goodbye

your affectionate M. ROSA

Today, Mary's day, may she grant me this grace!5

1 The document Sr. A. Crocifissa could not find among her papers is the deed of sale of a house in Cortemaggiore, drawn up in Piacenza on 10.4.1874 between M. Rosa and Signora Maddalena Parmigiani.

2 She had given it to her to show Canon Biagini, so that he could see the terms and conditions required by Parmigiani (she).

3 ... the green band: the green cover. The document is in AFSA, Causa

Parmigiani Maddalena.

4 M. Rosa found it again a few days later; cf. L 426,4.

5 Feast of the Presentation of the Virgin Mary.

She asks permission to take over the Orphanage from the Sisters of Providence. She sets out her conditions for accepting it.

A.M.F.

[Most Reverend Excellency]

1. Having been invited by the Rev. Superior of the Magdalens1 to see whether we could take over their Orphanage, as the Magdalens can no longer continue, I sent two of our sisters to visit the premises and see what was involved; they would have called on Your Most Reverend Excellency had they not had to leave at once for Milan.

2. They neither negotiated nor decided anything, however, because it is our practice, before opening a house and negotiating for it, to submit the matter to the Ordinary, and contracts are always made by common agreement.

3. Had my poor health and the cold season not prevented me, I would have come in person to submit humbly to Your Most Reverend Excellency all that, in my very small understanding, I think should be done. As I cannot do so in person, I shall try to do it as best I can on this sheet.

4. That the house be made over to us by way of sale to two of our sisters, with everything belonging to the Orphanage. That the whole administration be made over to us, together with everything needed for the girls' full maintenance, since we must continue the good running of the Orphanage; and any further conditions Your Most Reverend Excellency sees fit to add.2

Prostrating myself at your feet and asking for your Pastoral blessing, I remain, full of veneration, Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 Sr. Teodora Rusca, House of Providence, Lodi, had written to her. AFSA,

Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. ... , ,

2 She also declares herself willing to accept other conditions required by the

Bishop.

She should look after herself and call the doctor. She should pray.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear of your illness; for pity's sake look after yourself, see the doctor1 and make a triduum to the Sacred Heart.

I am stopping because I am unwell. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

1 She had written that she was ill but did not want to call the doctor.

She has done everything well.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Fever and headache have prevented me from answering yours.1 You have done everything well. Yes, let us pray.

Give my warm greetings to Sr. A. Sempliciana and believe me for ever your affectionate M. ROSA

1 She had written on 14 November about the orphanage and the municipal school, begging for a word confirming what she had decided.

Encouragement. She does not write at length because she is extremely busy and tired.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear a great deal, all the things you tell me about the Parrocchietta; blessed be God that so many troubles can be sweetened with a spoonful of sugar!1

2. Courage! I must write little because I have a headache.

Oh! How many letters! It frightens me; from morning to night always 8-10 hours at the desk!!2 Oh! Dear daughter, goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 I hear all the news. There is no lack of trouble, but with God's help it is light.

2 The correspondence piles up every day and she deals with it punctually, sparing no effort. Cf. L 362,1; 400,2.

She sends her the certificates. She has much work and is in poor health. She asks whether the sisters leaving for the other hospitals must have the modified habit. Greetings, blessings and exhortations to the Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you a copy of the certificates the Nizza doctor made out for you;1 as for Sr. A. Annunziata's, they have written that they will send them and they have not yet arrived; I have sent you a copy because I fear they may be lost, as they are, since you know one cannot rely on such distances.

2. I hope you have received my two registered letters and will see that I have answered all your questions.2

3. If you knew how many tasks, my dear, how much work I have, and always unwell, especially my head, which one can now call a daily pain! In short, it never leaves me.

4. Tell me whether you want cloth to make overcoats like ours. Tell me, I want to know whether the other Sisters to be sent to the other two hospitals3 really must have a habit like yours or whether we can keep our own, which I would much prefer, because, what can I say? I cannot get used to the idea that we are not uniform.4 Think about it. I believe it was rather Father Rocchi's way of thinking; what do you say?

5. Oh! Dear daughter, when a fortnight goes by without letters from you a world of anxiety wakes in me. For pity's sake, write.

6. Tell Sr. A. Rosa that I shall write to her soon,5 and meanwhile I send her a thousand blessings from Heaven, and likewise to all the Sisters; I thank them for their kind words and assure them they are exceedingly dear to me. So give them my love and tell them I hope to hear that they have settled in, that they have given all their care to the one thought of sanctification, have left behind every other idea and have taken up the exact observance of their Constitutions.6 And you, my dearest, take care of yourself and believe me yours for ever

affectionate M. ROSA G.

1 These are the certificates of competence in nursing and pharmacy issued to Sr. A. Giuseppa by the doctor of the Nizza hospital. They were needed in order to take charge of the pharmacy in the La Paz hospital.

2 They are L 389 and 408.

3 The hospitals of Sucre and Potosí.

4 The Sisters in La Paz had adopted a variation of the habit.

5 This is the Novice Sr. A. Rosa Telleria, who received the habit of the Daughters of St

Anne on 30 August 1879. Cf. L 435,4. She died in Piacenza on 5.8.1884. Cf. Index

IV,17.

6 ... have left behind any idea of being temporary and committed themselves to observing the Constitutions.

She should send two Sisters, one to Gualdo Tadino and the other to Spello. She will replace them as soon as possible.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, please send Sr. A. Leonina to Gualdo Tadino at once, and if you have a strong cook for Spello, they could travel together as far as Foligno, and then the Foligno one would take each to her place.1

2. She must be really strong for the kitchen. Sr. A. Leonina is to be assistant in the Infant School. Tell her to do well.

3. Listen, I shall soon send you two others, very good ones, and you will see you are pleased. Be patient; it is absolutely necessary that they go now.

4. I have not yet received the chestnuts, but I hope they will come. Oh! What scarcity we have in these parts!2 Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. I have found the papers3

1 ... then the Superior at Foligno, Sr. A. Guglielma Merli, would take them to their destination.

2 Cf. 438,1-3.

3 Cf. L 420.

She will send the Sisters as soon as possible. Instructions about the refectorian.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say about the sister;1 as soon as I can I shall send them, and then you can put Sr. A. Cesarina in the refectory or wherever you think best, spelling it out to her2 that what is left on the table cannot be eaten by the refectorian, nor by anyone, and especially not by the refectorian, who must keep everything, as she is responsible for it. Take care of yourself and believe me your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Cesarina, assistant to the boarders, neglects her duty and ignores the Superior's warnings.

2 spelling it out to her: telling her very clearly how she must behave.

She will send her two Sisters to help. She should try to take care of herself.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear about Sr. A. Sabina. Patience!1 Listen, if you want a cook I shall send you one as soon as I have her, together with the sister for the girls.

2. So try not to overdo it and take care of yourself. Do not work in the kitchen, because the strain will harm you.2 Goodbye, I am in a hurry; your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Sabina had caught smallpox; a bad cough followed and she cannot leave her bed.

2 Two Sisters were missing and there was always so much work, both for the girls and in the house, and the Superior also had to work in the kitchen.

She is in poor health. She should take courage. Always united in Jesus.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. Just one line, because I am not too well; I was in bed for two days. Oh! my head!1 Enough; take courage and try not to grieve over the distance,2 for at the feet of sweetest Jesus we are close together day and night. Oh! sweet Jesus!

Goodbye; greetings to all your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Headaches often afflicted her. Cf. L 414,4.

2 The Sister had asked to come to Piacenza. Cf. L 415,1.

She will send her two Sisters, but asks her to release one.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you really want a sister;1 but listen, you have one who knows how to pull teeth; well, we could2 do this: I would send you two and you would send me the one who pulls teeth; what do you say?3 The ones I have are really good, and you would be pleased.

Write to me and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

1 She had asked for a needlework teacher.

2 potressimo: we could.

3 The Superior is surprised at this humble tone and complains to the

Mother: "... why ask for the Sister so humbly?... You are my dear

Mother and must speak to me in the imperative, otherwise your letters cause me too much pain." Cf. L 5.12.1879.

Permission has been obtained to celebrate the three Masses at midnight on Christmas in our houses.

A.M.F.

Dearest Superior.

1. Permission has been obtained from Rome to celebrate all three

Masses at midnight on Holy Christmas in all our houses, provided the Ordinary consents.

2. We shall send you a copy of the brief1 later, as we cannot do so now for lack of time.

3. Take this letter, or send it, to the Bishop and ask for his consent. I remain

your most affectionate Mother Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The "brief", the document granting the faculty, is dated 11 December 1879.

She sends her the needlework teacher.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. Here is the skilled needlework teacher,2 a good assistant, whom I commend to you so that she can continue to study. Are you pleased? Have I served you well? Goodbye

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is taken from the Superior's reply: 7 December 1879.

2 Here is the promised teacher. Cf. L 397,2; 428,1.

Transfers of some Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. In haste, here is the address! Bedini Sisters, Borgo Castiglione No. 3, Bologna.1 I shall telegraph you when to send her.2 I shall also see about removing Sr. A. Cesarina;3 the other one, for now, be patient! As for Cherubina,4 do not send her to the sick, because she has an enormous belly, quite a sight, poor thing! But I shall see about placing her somewhere. Be patient. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 This was the boarding house where she and the sisters used to stay when travelling,

when a stop was needed. Cf. L 254, n. 4.

2 The sister being transferred, the one able to pull teeth, was to stop at this boarding house. Cf. L 430,1.

3 Cf. L 427,1.

4 Sr. A. Cherubina Massei was unwell.

She should accept the postulants and keep them, but if that is not possible she will have them come to Piacenza. News.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Just one [word]. Yes, accept all the postulants. If you could keep them with you for a while, tell me whether you can; otherwise I shall have them come here and arrange for them to be accompanied, but not by you, because it is indescribably cold here and you could fall ill.

2. So wait for me.1 And about the Canon, have you nothing to tell me?2 Be cheerful, for we shall see each other soon.

3. You will see from the circular that you have permission to have three Masses said.3 Goodbye; I am swamped with work. Goodbye your affectionate M. ROSA

1 So they would meet when she went to Pistoia.

2 And about the Canon... Cf. L 409,1-2.

3 Cf. L 431.

She sends documents and letters for her to forward to the addressees. She has a great deal of work. She gives news of Canon Biagini.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to you too, to tell you I have written to the Bishop and enclose what you ask for, which I think will suffice; for Lima

I have also sent the Delegate in Lima these papers that I am sending you.2

So you too try to get them to him; if it is

God's will, we shall go there; let us hope.3 All for Jesus, isn't it?

2. Here, my dear, we have a tremendous amount of work; I have no breathing space.

3. In one of your letters you asked about the Canon and the maid; I tell you they are just the same, and worse. Oh! what a business, my dear! Let us pray for them, for it is needed,4 as for me, who am truly wretched and laden with sins.

4. I am also writing a couple of lines to Rosa,5 but you know I do not know Spanish, so you will translate it for her. Goodbye. For pity's sake, take care of yourself and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 In the L of 1 November 1879 Sr. A. Giuseppa had told her of the

Apostolic Delegate in Lima's wish "to have the authentic deed of recognition of the Institute and a copy of the conditions required by the S. Congregation".

3 If it is God's will, she will accept the proposal with full readiness to respond to Jesus' love.

4 The Mother had given her news of the two. Cf. L 357,6 and the related note.

5 Cf. L 425,6.

She tells her the Count is coming to draw up the contract. She herself will come in January.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am letting you know that the Count2 will be there on Wednesday the 10th at 8 in the evening; he will stay wherever you decide and will remain in Pistoia as long as Doctor Chiappelli thinks necessary. But briefly, because he wants to leave.

2. For the rest, I shall come early in January. Keep everything for me,3 which I shall collect if God keeps me alive. Send me the two Postulants together with Sr. A. Restilde;4 I would like them to arrive by day. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 The Count... cf. L 409,2.

3 The whole cash surplus.

4 Sr. A. Restilde Colombo. She had been suffering from consumption for some time, but tried to keep up her courage and overcome the illness. Cf. L 409, n. 5 and L 439,1.

She sends a document. Various instructions and news. Greetings.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I am sending you Sr. A. Annunciata's certificate; I hope you have received yours, are pleased with them, and that they are as you wished.2

2. I hear what you tell me about poor Sr. A. Lucia. My God! How sad!3 I am always anxious and it pains me greatly when I have no letters from you; I would like to have them at least every fortnight. For pity's sake, do not leave me without them.

3. As for accepting houses, that is, hospitals, I wrote to you that they should make contracts the same as yours made in Bolivia.4

4. Send me the money and I shall send you the sisters by themselves; there is no need for priests or friars. They would travel alone and would certainly suffer less. I hope you have received everything.5 So write to me and, if you can, send me something, especially to pay the bill for the scotch cloth and ... Oh! what poverty there is this year; it is dreadful!6 Sr. A. Gabriella is here and sends you warm greetings, and Onorata too; they send their love; they are well, by God's mercy!7 Listen, you will find here a note from Father Alessandro.

5. Listen, write a little to our Bishop, especially as he is our protector; give him plenty of news. The Bishop there has written to him and says many fine things about you; clearly he loves you dearly. Oh! how good he is, and you can see he is truly a Father to you. Greet him for me and tell him I shall write to him soon.8

6. Take care of yourself, and the sisters too, that they do not wear themselves out. Do you understand? and that they do not fall ill; and send me the money soon, so that I can send the sisters at once, and with more of you9 you will not have to toil so much. Do you understand? look after your health, for pity's sake; greet everyone for me, and believe me for ever

affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. We have obtained permission to celebrate all three midnight Masses in the secondary houses as well.10 Listen, find out what is needed to be able to telegraph. Goodbye

your affectionate M. ROSA

2 Certificate of nursing and pharmacy service of Sr. A. Annunciata Chiodelli. Cf. L 425,1.
