A. Scolastica Barelliani on 28 February and Sr. A. Modesta Molesti on 6 March. Cf.

L 291, n. 1.

4 She explained this fully in L 408.

5 She refers to the cloth sent to her. Cf. L 389, n. 10.

6 That is why she asks her to pay the bill. Cf. L 438,1-3.

7 Sr. A. Gabriella Cavassa, the Mother House cook, and Onorata Colli.

8 Cf. L 408, n. 19.

9 e sante = being more numerous ...

10 The rescript is dated 11 December 1879. Cf. L 431.

They have a great deal of extra work, as every day they prepare and distribute a thousand bowls of soup to the poor.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am not writing in my own hand1 because I have no time. For a week we have had an immense amount of work here.

2. Every day a thousand bowls of soup are given out to the poor, and preparing them takes all our strength.

3. It is an act of charity by our Bishop together with other devout people to relieve in part the great poverty here.2

4. Do not send Sr. A. Lucia here any more;3 now that she is content, keep her there and see that Sr. A. Eletta does not tire of teaching her. If she wants, she can instruct her well; it all depends on her willingness. I bless you all affectionate Mother

1 It is written by Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega.

2 In the hardship caused by the severe famine, the Church of Piacenza,

led by Bishop G. B. Scalabrini, mobilised to help the needy. Mother

Rosa answered the appeal and the community worked actively: it takes all our strength.

3 Sr. A. Lucia Ferrari is the daughter of the Mayor of Castelnuovo Bormida.

She tells her of Sr. A. Restilde's holy and beautiful death. Gaspare has not been able to leave. If his presence is needed, she should telegraph.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line amid an abyss of business. The sister arrived safely,1 but the next day, after repeated haemorrhages, she gave up her soul to God! But she was attended by both spiritual and bodily physicians, and was very content. She died like a saint, and the confessor was beside himself at seeing so beautiful a soul. She received everything, and joyfully.2

2. Gaspare has not yet been able to come; if you really see a need, he will leave at once.3 Telegraph, and he will come sooner.

3. Goodbye; I am busy; we are distributing 1000 bowls of soup a day.4 Goodbye

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Restilde Colombo. Cf. L 436, n. 4.

2 She received every spiritual and bodily aid with the joy of a bride going to meet the Bridegroom.

3 Cf. L 436,2.

4 Cf. L 438,1-3.

She praises her apostolic zeal and encourages her; she asks her to help with the quarterly rent of the house in vicolo Margana.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you tell me about... the Children of Mary. Oh! blessed be God who knows so well how to inspire my daughter! So courage! For pity's sake, never lose heart.

2. Listen, I am writing little because I am truly overwhelmed with work and have no breathing space.2

3. Oh! The poor who groan!3 Listen, if you and the one at the Fornaci had a little money to add to the Margana rent, I would try to send the rest. What a winter! I assure you it makes me sigh.4

4. I don't [know] when I shall come to Rome, because the Bishop does not want me to go; so certainly not in January!

Goodbye, yours

affectionate M. ROSA

1 There was a good number of Children of Mary at the Parrocchietta. Sr. A. Celsa taught and encouraged them.

2 Cf. L 424,2.

3 She is short of money and tries to help the poor as much as possible.

Cf. L 328,4.

4 She asks whether she can contribute, together with the Superior of the School in via delle Fornaci, to the rent of the House in vicolo Margana, which was high: 825 lire a quarter, payable in advance. Cf. Lettere 4, p. 657.

A.M.F.

Dear Daughter,

1. I cannot understand why all the Sister's things have not yet reached you. We shall write today; what patience is needed! Goodbye, in haste, a big hug in dear Jesus, where I leave you, and I am yours for ever

affectionate M. R.

Happy Christmas; one of the little Infants each2 in return for your good wishes.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A thousand thanks for your gift in the registered letter.1

I should like to tell you so many things, but oh! what a burden of work, it is immense! Be patient and remember that at the feet of my Jesus I always hold you close; and you, love me and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

She sets out the harmful consequences of her leaving the community to visit her father. Reminding her of the duty to follow "Jesus, the most lovable", she invites her to choose and awaits her answer.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Overwhelmed as I am with work, I send you two lines in reply to yours. You weep and want to satisfy a natural affection, that is, to go and see your father. I have nothing against it, but! the consequences will certainly be far more painful for you.1

2. First, because you would be leaving a number of girls who are all barely stuck together with spit, and the responsibility before God is entirely yours.2

3. Oh! daughter! the flesh ends with worms; the spirit and sacrifice fly to God! so? choose!

4. Jesus said to Peter: leave father and mother, come and follow me. So what do you say? Which of the two do you want to follow? Jesus or the flesh?3 I am sure that it will be Jesus, the most lovable, who conquers and triumphs in your heart. Away with natural affections, and let us give proof of what we tell him every day: that for him we want to make every sacrifice.

5. In short, a thousand affectionate words. Enough. Love Jesus and seek him alone; you will see, dear daughter, that you will be content; you will see it, yes,4 my dear daughter. So? I await your letter and am

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The consequences will then make you suffer even more. Sr. A. Celsa had tasks of great responsibility: Superior of the community, head of the

School, teacher, and assistant to the Children of Mary.

2 Girls stuck together with spit: insecure, not well formed, in need of strong guidance and discipline.

3 The flesh ends with worms... Jesus or the flesh: expressions shaped by the dualistic outlook of the time.

4 The final soaring note: in love for Jesus she will find joy, yes.

II. INDEX OF ADDRESSEES OF THE LETTERS

1. ANDREOTTI (Fr Ottavio) RAFFAELE, born at Piteglio (Pistoia) on 10.1.1837, entered the Congregation of the Piarists on 28.3.1855. After a suitable period as a teacher he continued his clerical studies and was ordained priest at Castelfiorentino. He met M. Rosa and Fr Tornatore in Florence, where he taught at the San Carlo; he formed ties of friendship and wished to be, and was, "associated" with the FSA Institute, as an archive document shows. Cf. AFSA, Foundation Florence. For over forty-five years he devoted himself to teaching, distinguishing himself as an accomplished Christian educator. He died on 25 July 1903 after a painful illness. L 162.

2. BARBIELLINI AMIDEI (Count) GASPARE. Born in Rome on 6.7.1851, he died there on 26.9.1931. In 1876 he married Carlotta Custo and had six children by her: Maria Adelaide (1877-1908), Rosetta (1879-1881), Camillo Raffaele (1881-1909), Federica Annina (1885-1980), Emilia (1891-1944), Bernardo (1896-1940). M. Rosa loved him as a son and held him in esteem, entrusting him with various Institute matters, as several letters in this volume show: Cf. L 155, n. 4; 291,3; 352,3. On 10 January 1877 she appointed him her general attorney (AFSA, Deed Monti Domenico registered in Rome on 12 January 1877). The appointment was revoked in 1896 because of his administrative failings. After M. Rosa's death Barbiellini continued to press financial claims against the Institute and brought lawsuits against it. Cf. Positio Super Virtutibus, p. 770 ff. Letters published here: 4; 7; 53; 222; 228; 230; 235; 236; 237; 238; 243; 253.

3. BARISIONI (Sr. A. Teodora) MARIA, daughter of Giuseppe and Rosa Resecco, born at Ovada on 23.3.1852. She received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne on 29.9.1874 and made her first vows on 26.7.1877. She served in various houses of the Institute in different tasks. She died in Bari on 26.2.1947. L 176.

4. BARZANÒ (Sr. A. Maurizia) GIUSEPPINA. Born to Paolo and Teresa Fontana at Brugherio (Milan) on 28.2.1841, she entered the Institute on 24.7.1875, received the habit on 26.8.1875 and made her first vows on 26.7.1877. After a period of training at Bagnacavallo she was at Nizza Monferrato, superior of the Community from 1878 to 1886, and later in other hospital communities: Crotone, Busseto. In 1913 she testified at the rogatory process in Piacenza on Mother Rosa's virtues. She was then Superior of the Gargatano Community, where she died on 23.4.1930. L 54; 73; 98; 101.

5. BELLARDO (Sr. A. Panasia) TERESA. She received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne on 23.1.1872. She was given teaching posts in various elementary schools of the Institute: Ferrara, Rome, Pennabilli; at Appignano in 1879, besides running the School, she was also Superior of the community. She asked and obtained leave to go to the missions and was sent to Bolivia in 1883. After three years she left the Institute. L 329.

6. BENNICELLI (Father) ANTONIO. Born in Rome on 18.12.1817, he died there on 31.12.1895. He entered the Order of Clerks Regular, Ministers of the Sick (Camillians) on 20.10.1832, made his profession on 21.6.1834 and was ordained priest on 26.4.1840 at Viterbo. He held various posts in his religious Family: secretary and general consultor, bursar in several communities. From 1855 to 1890 he was parish priest of the church of St Mary Magdalene (attached to the generalate). From 1855 he was president of the Congregation of Noble Ladies of Mary Assumed into Heaven. In 1865 he founded the "House for Penitent Women" in via dei Riarii in the Lungara. In 1878 he wished to donate this institution to the Daughters of Saint Anne. Negotiations began but were not concluded (Cf. L 190) because of the unfavourable conditions, as the Foundress clearly pointed out to him (Cf. Index IV, p. 679). L 190.

7. CAMPORESI (Sr. A. Eufemia) CLEMENTINA. Born at Galleate (Forlì) on 31.3.1856, she joined the FSA on 18.8.1873 and received the habit on 30.9.1873. After a short time in the Nizza Monferrato community she was at Foligno and later teacher and superior at S. Martinello, Parma and Appignano. Having fallen ill she was transferred to the Mother House at Piacenza, then to the house for the sick in Via della Morte, where she died in July 1878. L 3.

III. INDEX OF NOTABLE PERSONS NAMED IN THE CORRESPONDENCE

1. ACCINELLI (Canon) ANTONIO. Volumes 3 and 4 of M. Rosa Gattorno's Letters highlighted the figure of this zealous and energetic Genoese priest, close to the Gattorno family and Mother Rosa's attorney for her father's inheritance, and brought out the part he played in the communities of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Liguria and Piedmont. In 1878-79 his dedication knows no pause, moved as he is by the "bond of friendship" with the Mother Foundress, by fidelity to his priestly mission and by devotion to Saint Anne, which becomes active service to the work of her Daughters, to "build them up in spirit and in material things". This is borne out by his 59 letters to M. Rosa from this period, by the Mother's remarks, brief and occasional though they are, to the superiors and sisters of Genoa, Sampierdarena and Sestri, and by their correspondence with the Mother. There are also hints of friction with the young superior of Genoa, softened however by M. Rosa: "Try to treat him well, as he deserves". Cf. L 114,2. The other letters mentioning him in the text or notes are: L 6,2; 74, n. 4; 79, n. 1; 99,2 and n. 3; 114,2 and nn. 4-5; 120,2; 217,1; 223,1 and n. 1; 348,2; 361,2,3,4,5 and n. 3; 382,4. Cf. 2. CUSTO ALESSANDRO. Mother Rosa's letters to her son Alessandro from 1878-79 are missing; the correspondence between mother and son is barely touched on in the Mother's letters to the superiors of the Florence and Rome houses, where the young man lived during these two years. Explicit and frequent, by contrast, is news of his poor health, his work, his problems and troubles: sorrow upon sorrow, "stabs" in the Mother's heart. Towards the end of 1877 Alessandro is in Florence, taken on for an unpaid trial period at the Banca Subalpina. He visits the FSA house at via Faenza 54, receiving advice and material help (L 67,1; 104,3). But his traineeship at the bank does not go well, owing to his poor health and equally weak will. Early in January 1879 he goes to Rome to have things out with his mother: he wants a job in Rome and will hear no more of Florence. Yet the Bank's Director, after reporting his failings — unjustified absences and improper conduct at the office — is willing to take him on, provided he changes his ways. But something else wounds the mother's heart: he is living with a young woman and passing her off as his wife. He needs money and claims rights over the property. The Mother answers him firmly and will not be blackmailed or frightened (L 228), but she suffers "a grief that, of all that can be put together, is the greatest"; a grief sharpened by his disappearance and continued silence. She has Sr. A. Santina Solenghi look for him in Florence (L 233; 239) and entrusts herself, as always, to the Lord. She prays and asks for prayers "for the conversion of a sinner very dear to her heart" (L 241, 9; 245,1,4-5; 246,4; 249, n. 4). Having moved to Rome, Alessandro gets back in touch with his mother. He makes her "suffer with his conduct, without work, without money and ill. Sr. A. Illuminata (Cavassa) looks after him in everything, but believe me, for me he is a painful thorn". So the mother wrote to Sr. A. Santina Solenghi on 24.2.1879 (L 255,5). A month later she has something consoling to say. He has promised to mend his ways: "now he is making the Holy retreat with the friars, God grant he may be converted" (L 267,2). The Mother's later correspondence makes no mention of Alessandro. From letters written to her by Sup. Illuminata we know that in April he married the young woman he lived with. Towards the end of 1879 he is at Alatri, in the province of Frosinone, with her and working for himself. In an undated L (probably from 1880) to Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, the mother says she is pleased with her son: "Alessandro is really well settled. He has taken a wife and has a son. He is so good, truly religious, and an edification to all. He has set up a fine factory and I hope that in a few years he will no longer need anyone and will be able to give..."
