IV. THE FOUNDATIONS (1878-1879)

The Houses are listed in chronological order of opening.

1. S. LUCA D'ALBARO (Genoa).

Home nursing - School

At S. Luca d'Albaro the Daughters of Saint Anne, nurses from the Genoa community, would go at the request of some family to look after a sick person. To make their service easier, some local ladies proposed to M. Rosa that she station her daughters there permanently to teach the children and nurse the sick at home. They offered a small flat and undertook to help them with a subsidy.

It was arranged with Fr Antonio Accinelli to move the furniture from the Staglieno house, which the FSA had left on 10.12.1877 (Cf. Lettere 4, p. 661). Meanwhile M. Rosa had chosen the Sisters and asked Superior Amabile Montanari of the Genoa Nurses' House to accompany them. Cf. L 6. They went there on 1*8 January 1878 with that Superior: Sr. A. Beata Torriani as superior, Sr. A. Fausta Torriani for the school, Sr. A. Restilde Colombo and, a few days later, Sr. A. Davidina Butterani, to care for the sick.

The Parish Priest welcomed them warmly and promised his support. Providence came to meet them with an offer from the Rivara ladies: £ 50 for initial expenses. They soon began nursing a sick lady, but the school had to wait for summer and the influx of holidaymakers. They went on in sacrifice and poverty, so that the Mother, worried, entrusted those heroic daughters of hers to her friend Anna Grasso, who took them to heart. The school opened in February with 6 girls. Over time the number grew, but not by much. The promised subsidy for the school was never paid, so M. Rosa asked Fr Accinelli to intervene and, having heard from him that she was free to act as she saw fit since he had made no commitment as to duration, she charged him with withdrawing the Sisters. On 5.11.1878 he informed her in these terms: The Albaro house is closed, the Rivara ladies are resigned, tomorrow the things will be collected. For a sick woman they were caring for, help will continue to be sent from Genoa. Cf. AFSA. D. 2. 11, B. 4. 95.

2. MONTORIO AL VOMANO (Teramo). Nursery School

Negotiations for sending the FSA to take charge of the children's education at Montorio, a farming town in the province of Teramo, were conducted between Mother Rosa and the president of the local Charity Congregation, Dr Teodosio Scarselli. A firm believer in the primary importance of educating children of every class, he had conceived the Nursery School as early as 1866, but could launch his project only in 1877, when he obtained from the Town Council an old building that could be adapted for school use and the official resolution of the Congregation. He then wrote to the Foundress of the FSA, explaining the purpose of the work and asking for three Sisters with the necessary qualifications. On receiving a positive answer he had the premises prepared as their lodging, and the date of their arrival was fixed to coincide with the School's opening. Sr. A. Eugenia Gaudenzi, the superior, Sr. A. Innocenza Bergamini and Sr. A. Pancrazia Maspero arrived on 28 April 1878. On 5 May the infant school opened with 60 children aged 3 to 5, rising after three days to 100, which remained the steady attendance in following years too. The inauguration, held with great solemnity and participation (300 people crowded the school, among them the civil and school authorities of the town and province), was a historic day for Montorio. Noteworthy were the speeches of the Mayor and of Dr Scarselli, who spoke of the importance of education and of the plan to complete it by constructing a "dedicated building with accommodation for the teaching staff". The Sisters adapted willingly to local life. Each morning they went out to Church; they spent almost the whole day at school with the children and returned home towards evening. The people loved and esteemed them. Dr Scarselli himself, who regarded the school as his own creation, valued their central role and full cooperation in the all-round formation of the pupils, who at the end of the course were found ready for the second elementary class. In his correspondence with the Foundress he praises the Sisters, calling them "benefactresses. They have always met with applause and goodwill, for I have not failed to cover the shortcomings of one or another", he wrote to her on 10.2.1886. On 5.9.86 M. Rosa, in view of the Sisters' demanding work, asked for the contract to be renewed with a fourth Sister taken on and the salary raised; otherwise she would be forced to withdraw them. The answer was no. Three were enough; a raise was impossible for lack of funds, which had been absorbed by the construction of the building begun three years earlier and still unfinished. So a decision was reached, painful for both sides but irrevocable. The FSA remained at Montorio al Vomano from April 1878 until the end of the 1885-1886 school year.

Cf. AFSA. FcIC. Reg. Prot. 1876-81. D. 2. 12.

3. BORGO S. DONNINO - FIDENZA (Parma). Hospital

On 1.6.1878 the President of the "Administration of Civil Hospices" informed Mother Rosa Gattorno of the Commission's decision to entrust the internal service of the town's civil hospital to five FSA from the following 1 July. The earlier oral agreements between M. Rosa and the representatives of the Board were followed by others to finalise the Agreement, which both parties signed on 22.6.1878. The document sets out clearly the aspects and scope of the internal service — housekeeping, nursing, kitchen — entrusted to the "pious sodality", as well as their role and relations with the medical, auxiliary and administrative staff. Of basic importance is point 4, expressly wanted by the Mother to avoid the unfortunate problems that had arisen with various Administrations. It reads: "The Administration, aware that it is entrusting the service of the hospital not to individual persons but to a pious sodality, declares that it will never sever the bonds uniting these persons to the body to which they belong; thus the Mother General shall always be free to change the staff serving this hospital and replace them with others". It then stresses the Administration's right to ask the Mother General for the "recall of any persons who seem to need recalling and replacing by others". Mother Rosa, on the appointed date, 1 July 1878, accompanied the five Sisters. We learn this from a letter she wrote to Sr. A. Santina Solenghi on 29 June: "... for your information, on Monday (1 July) I leave... I am going to Borgo (S. Donnino), Bologna and Ferrara, then Piacenza". Cf. L 90,4. She had appointed Sr. A. Camilla Valentini superior and director. The other four are named in the superior's correspondence with the Mother, to whom she sent detailed reports on how the service was going. In a letter from the first days (undated) she names Sr. A. Battistina (Bertuzzi), Sr. A. Annunziata (Aliverti), Sr. A. Daria (Negri) and Sr. A. Cristina (Persini). Superior Camilla's "breaking-in" cost her great effort and some strain: "Oh, how distressed I am these days at having too little ability! for I still do not properly understand the regulations of this hospital... I am afraid of not doing well... believe me, my Mother, I truly want to do it, but I cannot manage... now everything is in our charge... I told the bursar, who is still here, to do the dietary (the diet) of the patients himself as well" (L n.d.). The sisters have so much to do. Besides the patients to nurse, a daily average of 24-26, there is the extra work at the start: an inventory of everything. In reporting to the Mother on their service she also tells her the timetable of community prayers: 5-5.45 meditation; 6 Holy Mass; 11.30 prayers; 14 reading; 14.30 chaplet of the Lord; 20 rosary. Everything well organised at a brisk pace. "Evening comes and we are tired," she writes again on 20.8.1878, "but we are always cheerful; let all be for God and nothing for us". The Mother watches over and guides the little community, writing often to the superior or calling her to Piacenza. The sisters make progress, and the superior shows excellent leadership. Four years later, in April 1882, the Mother calls her to Piacenza and entrusts her with a far wider mission: she will go to Bolivia with 11 Sisters. She will be the first Provincial Superior of the Institute's first-born missionary Province. In 1922 she will become the fourth Superior General.

Other FSA followed these first ones, sharing the life and history of the hospital for over a century until in 1986, the Institute's workforce having dwindled through the fall in vocations and the rising age of the active Sisters, the Superior General of the time reluctantly withdrew the few elderly Sisters who remained. They left the hospital on 30.9.1986, after 108 years.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-81. Foundations - Fidenza. M. Camilla Valentini, O. 45.

4. TERMINI IMERESE (Palermo). Orphanage - School

This is the second FSA "House" in Sicily, preceded by Agrigento two years earlier. It was the Archbishop of Palermo, Mgr Michelangelo Celesia, who began the negotiations with the Mother Foundress and brought them to a close. Unable to meet her in Piacenza, he wrote to her in Rome on 16.2.78 conveying the wish of the Board of the S. Pietro orphanage "to have two Sisters to direct those pupils who until now have been almost left to themselves". He adds that the financial means of the "establishment are not very prosperous, but arrangements have nevertheless been made to ensure the upkeep of the new Superiors". M. Rosa is not concerned about the finances but about the girls "almost left to themselves" and about her own sisters, who must number no fewer than three to live faithfully by the Rules and spirit of the congregation. On 3 April the Archbishop replies, agrees on the number and settles some details, including when they will come. On 11 May he sends the money for the journey. Having sailed from Genoa on 8.7.78 (cf. L 97), Sr. A. Gaudenzia Martinelli, Sr. A. Sempliciana Saviotti and Sr. A. Geltrude Branchi reach Palermo on 12 July, but must wait because the Board member of the Termini orphanage who is to accompany them is detained. Meanwhile they attend the celebrations in honour of St Rosalia, and finally on 17.7.1878 they reach their destination. The welcome is festive, in the style of a religious solemnity: in the adjoining church of S. Pietro, a Te Deum of thanksgiving, Holy Mass and Eucharistic benediction; then the presentation of the orphans housed there — 54 of them, little ones, older girls and elderly women — and a tour of the premises. From the first moment the sisters realise the difficulties and the great labour awaiting them in breaking up that uncultivated, chaotic field. In her first report to the Mother the Superior is terse: "you cannot imagine the poverty, the wickedness and the ambition of this orphanage". Each one adapts and manages as best she can; those with a good appetite ask their relatives for extra food or buy it on credit; each does her own washing, each keeps her rags, plates and cutlery under her own bed. There are three classes of people here: chronically ill old women... young women with fashionable hairstyles and ragged dresses... the little girls almost all in rags, without shifts, sheets or towels", and she adds: "poor souls, I truly pity them". She sets about putting things in order to suit the persons and the needs of each age. To the elderly she assigns a separate area with their "Superior", who had led them and retains a certain moral standing. The same for the young women and the little girls, who are "provided with everything". Order, cleanliness, timetables and adequate food are the pillars of the new organisation, which however demands a great deal of work; three Sisters are clearly not enough. The Mother urges the Board to accept a fourth. They agree, but for financial reasons can pay only her journey (L 111); her upkeep will fall to the Institute. The Board members express satisfaction and readiness to make the necessary improvements and meet the cost, despite the Board's precarious finances. The superior keeps the Mother informed with frequent reports and asks for guidance as she organises the life of the community and the sisters, wanting to know "whether you are pleased and whether it is right" in everything, starting with the daily timetable. The Sisters rise at 4, meditation, prayers, Holy Mass at 6. At 8 school lessons begin, the sewing school and weaving; work resumes in the afternoon after the lunch break. The Sisters are beside the little ones and the older girls, helping them with personal hygiene, teaching them and giving them an all-round formation to prepare them for an upright and honest life. The Mother approves, encourages and advises, writing in her own hand; she also presses the Board to avoid "increasing the work" and insists on a summer rest (L 387. 412). When at the start of the new school year (1878-79) the municipal school for day pupils and boarders is opened in the orphanage and entrusted to the Sisters, the Mother applies for another teacher to be taken on (L 371). For the sisters' health she suggests suitable remedies and insists that they be well treated and cared for (L 191; 297; 387), letting them feel the warmth of her motherhood: "I am always beside you in mind and spirit". For their part the sisters live up to her teaching and to the hopes placed in them by the local authorities and the Archbishop. He expressed his approval by writing to the Foundress on 29.8.1878, thanking her for the "excellent choice of the persons sent. In a city as difficult as Termini they have already won everyone's admiration and the respect of the authorities and of all classes of citizens". In 1889 the Charity Congregation entrusted the Daughters of Saint Anne with the running of the Poorhouse, and in 1892 the President of the "Shelter for Poor Women under the title of St Lucy" asked M. Rosa for Sisters; after long negotiations three Daughters of Saint Anne began their mission as mothers and educators of very many girls who were doubly poor, being without family and without means of support. Five years later the two institutions were merged in the premises of the S. Pietro Institute under the name "S. Lucia - S. Pietro Orphanage", and remained in the care of the Daughters of Saint Anne until 1991.

AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-81. D. 2. 13, G. 1. 2.

5. NAPLES. "Refuge for Abandoned Girls" (Orphanage)

The President of the "Association for the Rehabilitation of Abandoned Girls", Cav. Francesco Martuscelli, together with a group of noble ladies of Naples, looked after abandoned or "at-risk" girls, placing them in various "Retreats" in the city and paying for their keep. Wishing to give them a single safe place for prevention, care and formation, he obtained part of the "Refuge for Abandoned Girls", whose Administrative Commission granted him its direction. He therefore wrote to Mother Rosa Gattorno on 10.5.1878 asking for three sisters: "one of greater authority, a sewing mistress and another... They would see to the housekeeping and everything else a mother must see to". The religious had been recommended to him by Marchioness Maria Mirelli, "most devoted to Saint Anne" and an admirer of her Daughters. She too worked to obtain them, made the proposal to the superior of the "Sannicandro House", Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti, and also wrote to the Foundress. In the Protocol Register 1878-1881 the details of the correspondence on this matter are carefully noted in the Mother's own hand. Once the house was ready and the conditions for the Sisters' service had been clarified on both sides, two Sisters, Evangelista Antoniazzi and Primitiva Boresi, arrived on 26 July 1878, accompanied by superior Palmira, and Cav. Martuscelli handed over to them, chosen from the 18 placed in other "Refuges", the first two girls, aged 13 years old; others gradually joined them while the superior was awaited. Meanwhile Sr. A. Olimpia Lupi had been added to the first two sisters for the kitchen; towards the end of August Sr. A. Desideria Aliprandi arrived as sewing mistress and superior. The number of "wayward" girls grew, and with them the problems and worries for the Sisters, who were young and almost the same age as some of the "seasoned" residents, capable of the most refined ruses to get round the iron discipline the Director firmly required; but the sisters could not bring themselves to act almost as jailers. The Director complained of this to the Mother in a "strictly confidential" letter of 17 December 1878: "No one admires more than I the goodness, self-denial and privations to which the Sisters I have had the honour of knowing submit themselves, but it grieves me that I cannot rely on their carrying out the instructions I give them...". In the end the Mother, during her visit to the Naples Houses at the end of January 1879, saw the situation for herself and agreed with Cav. Martuscelli to withdraw the Sisters. They left the "Refuge" on 9 February 1879.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-'81. Foundations Naples - "Reclusorio Derelitte". D. 2. 13.

6. BAGNOREA (Viterbo). Hospital

To look after and nurse the few patients (three on average) in the small "Civic Hospital" of Bagnorea (later Bagnoregio) the Mother Foundress sent Sr. A. Virginia Gaggi. She arrived on 1 August 1878 with two novices: Sr. A. Leonora Cavallini and Sr. A. Mirta Lemoggi. That same day the two "Sisters of Saint Anne of Providence", who had given commendable service there, handed over. They were withdrawing because their rule did not provide for such work, but they stayed on in the town School. Warmly welcomed by Bishop Mgr Raffaele Corradi, a Genoese Discalced Carmelite, the FSA set to work diligently. The superior was already experienced, and the others had a good training with her. Rising at 4.15; Holy Mass at 5.30 followed by meditation, because the hospital chaplain celebrated then and they had to keep to his times. The rest of the day followed the timetable of the other FSA communities. Nursing the patients by day and, in serious cases, by night, keeping the wards tidy and clean, was the sisters' task, and only exceptionally was an auxiliary called in, man or woman as needed. The hospital was reserved for the poorest people of the town, which had little more than 4,000 inhabitants, so that when there were no patients the Sisters had time to sew or embroider to order to supplement their meagre income: £ 750 a year for all three. The situation had been clearly explained to the Mother by Canon Nazzareno Pettirossi in correspondence from 2.5 to 18.7.1878, and she had accepted, since it was an episcopal hospital without sufficient income. The administrative commission, however, hoped to expand it over time. The sisters who followed one another there were excellent co-workers, inspired by a spirit of charity and self-denial. At the end of November 1920 the hospital moved premises and care improved with the hiring of a lay auxiliary. A surgical unit was later fitted out, in the hope also of financial gain, since finances were very precarious because of the costs of building the new premises. Consequently, to balance the budget it was decided among other things to reduce the nursing staff. The Administration asked Superior General M. Corredentrice Pomarici to amend the agreement, reducing the Sisters' presence to a single nurse. For obvious reasons the proposal was not accepted, and so the FSA ended their service at the hospital in April 1935. In 1924 the Bishop had asked for and obtained three Sisters for service at the Seminary. For financial reasons he reluctantly had to do without them, the seminarians having dwindled to a very small number.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Found. - Bagnorea. D. 2. 11.

7. S. MARIA CAPUA VETERE (Caserta). "S. Giuseppe Melorio" Hospital

In choosing a religious congregation to entrust with the service of the local hospital, the members of the "Administration of the Conservatory of S. Teresa del Carmine" had turned to the Daughters of Saint Anne, whom they knew through the printed letter the Sisters had addressed and circulated to benefactors soon after their arrival in Naples in May 1877 (cf. Lettere 4, L 385). Through Mgr Filippo D'Amico they contacted the superior of the "Sannicandro House" on 26.6.1878 and, on her advice, wrote to the

Mother Foundress asking for three sisters. The answer is yes: not three but five Sisters she is ready to assign, since "in hospitals we have not only the management but also the service, both the kitchen and all the services that can be done for a patient; we have no auxiliaries. Only a man for what modesty prevents us from doing for men". President Gaetano Saraceni for his part specifies the terms of the agreement, holding to three Sisters, since there is already lay staff as the regulations require; besides the usual board, lodging, etc., they will receive a combined monthly allowance of £ 45. The hospital, founded almost twenty years earlier through the never-failing charity of the faithful, will be able to prosper and grow thanks to the generous and effective cooperation of the sisters, who are inspired "by sentiments of piety and religion". The Mother promptly informs the Archbishop of Capua, Francesco Saverio Apuzzo, asking his pastoral blessing on the Daughters of Saint Anne coming to his diocese to serve the sick in charity. Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti, superior, Sr. A. Candida Fiori, nurse, and Sr. A. Assunta dell'Agnello, in charge of the kitchen, arrive on 23 August 1878, ready and willing to take on the "great deal to do". "They have put everything in our hands," the superior writes to the Mother. Linen to check, mend and complete; registers to reorganise; a kitchen to set up; a thorough cleaning of every room. These are the first extraordinary tasks, besides directing the service, the hospital administration and the care of the patients. Every day the President and the Medical Director visit and are pleased. "The sisters are loved and esteemed by all... and they speak very highly of our Institute". So superior Tommasina Viterbo wrote to Mother Rosa after visiting from Naples, where she was passing through on her way to open the house at Aci S. Antonio in Sicily. A relationship of esteem and trust grew up between the president and the Sisters. He later met the Mother when she visited in January 1879 (cf. L 235; 237; 328; 341), and held her in high regard, grateful for the Sisters' considerable contribution to the smooth running and growth of the hospital. He corresponded with her out of friendship and kinship in charity as well as for practical reasons. In 1889 he wished to found at his own expense an institution for poor and needy elderly people and could turn to no one but M. Rosa for effective and proven cooperation; she very gladly assigned four sisters, happy to extend the reach of her charity to the "Gaetano Saraceni" poorhouse. In 1896 the Administration of the "Melorio" hospital also asked for and obtained five of her religious, with the same duties as those working at the "S. Giuseppe". The FSA's work later extended to other areas of public welfare: the municipal pharmacy distributing medicines to the poor, the "Foundling Hospital", the "Cappabianca Institute for the Blind and Deaf-Mute". In 1939, with the merger of the two hospitals, the religious community was unified and enlarged. By common testimony the FSA "upheld the prestige of the hospital as an integral part of high and specific spiritual and professional quality". Sadly their presence ended in 1993 because of the Institute's well-known shortage of numbers, and their withdrawal was decided.

Cf. AFSA, Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - S. Maria C.V. D. 2. 13.

8. NAPLES. Parish Elementary School, "S. Teresa" Orphanage

The parish priest of S. Giacomo degli Italiani in Naples, wishing to give a human and Christian formation to the children of the parish, almost all of them poor, relied for financial and organisational help on the work of Marchioness Laura Balbi Caracciolo, one of his penitents, who wanted to set up a "fund" to run an elementary School and an orphanage (L 135). She therefore gladly accepted the post of director conferred on her by the parish priest and on 15 July 1878 wrote to Mother Rosa Gattorno asking for eight Sisters for these works and for visiting and nursing the sick at home. She had come to know the Daughters of Saint Anne in Naples and considered their cooperation necessary. On receiving a positive answer she prepares lodgings for them and for the orphans. She wishes, and presses the Mother, that the inauguration take place on 26 July. But as the Sisters are not ready she resigns herself to postponing it. They arrive on 22 August. On the 24th there is the solemn inauguration. Four little orphans are ready. The religious community is made up of: Sr. A. Veneranda Picco, superior, Sr. Quintina Gaudenzi, Paolina (?), Albina Garavaldi, Carla Cocchi, Ersilia

Valentini, Rachele Capricioni (L 135). The superior gets the community off to a good start, following the Mother's suggestions (L 135; 137; 145), and tries to cooperate with the Marchioness while standing firm in defending the autonomy of the religious community, for which she alone is responsible. She needs a good measure of prudence and tact in her daily dealings with the authoritarian lady, who clings to her own views with an unbending will to command. The Mother urges her to patience and firmness and resolves the overwork caused by the illness of some sisters by sending help (L 151; 153; 161; 210). Both school and boarding house are well under way, but tensions with the Marchioness grow, worsening after her break with the parish priest. He had contradicted her over a financial matter and had been pushed out. Moreover, the Sisters are consequently forbidden any contact with him. The superior, wanting sure guidance in running the work and unable to untangle by letter the knot of difficulties piling up day by day, asks and obtains from the Mother, with the Archbishop's prior consent, permission to go to Piacenza to consult her (L 320). On learning this the Marchioness denounces this act of insubordination to the Mother Foundress and informs her of her "inexorable resolution" to dismiss the Daughters of Saint Anne within a month (Cf. L to M. Rosa 27.6.1879). The Mother arranged for them to leave on 10 July 1879. The parish work came to an end. The Marchioness saw to placing the orphans in another institution. The parish priest begged the Mother to assign at least two Sisters to animate the parish's liturgical celebrations and Sunday catechesis.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. F. 5. 38. Foundations - Naples.

9. ROME - "House for Penitent Women"

Since 1 February 1877 the FSA have been in the building at Vicolo Margana 12, rented on a seven-year lease, continuing the home nursing of the sick and the educational work for girls carried on at their previous addresses, via della Lungara 46 and via Pettinari 64 (cf. Lettere 4, p. 656 ff.). But in little less than a year the work grows and the twelve rooms are inadequate and unsuitable for the school and boarding house. The community, which lived on alms, is also burdened by the high rent: £ 825 every quarter. Fr Antonio Bennicelli (cf. Index II, 6) learns of the problem and promises a solution with an ideal offer: to hand over to the FSA the "Pious Shelter House" in via dei Riari, which he had founded and directed. There is room there not only for the "penitent young women" whom the FSA would guard, educate and direct, but also for their present boarders and the school. The offer appeals to the Superior, Sr. A. Illuminata Cavassa, and to Sr. A. Agnese Sismondini, who hasten to tell the Mother of this favourable opportunity (L 110). Fr Bennicelli for his part writes to the Mother Foundress saying he is very glad to make the offer to her Institute (cf. L 6.10.1878). He has already offered the house to the Sisters of St Joseph of the Apparition, still serving in the "Pious House", but since they "do not wish to accept for the present" nothing prevents him from turning to other religious. He encloses a draft agreement, urging her to sign it as acceptance of the arrangement, which will be finalised later with the regular approval of the competent ecclesiastical authorities. He is anxious to conclude the matter. And since the Sisters of St Joseph, on learning of it, gave notice without due warning and left the house on the morning of 15 October, that same afternoon the ladies of the Pious Union hurriedly fetch the FSA sisters from the Vicolo Margana house to take their place. None of them had been able to visit the much-praised house, having always been refused for one reason or another. They had trusted the donor's assurances. But once inside they realise with astonishment and dismay that in that "reclusorium", run like a strictly enclosed monastery with grilles and bans on coming and going, there is indeed room for the Vicolo Margana boarders, but they would have to live alongside the other residents, the "penitents". What is needed instead is separate premises, which could be obtained by occupying part of the building now rented out and having renovation work done — costly work, moreover — at the expense of the Daughters of Saint Anne. The superior, Sr. A. Illuminata, who had accompanied the first Sisters — Sr. A. Agnese Sismondini, Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, Sr. A. Flora Boggiani — settles and guides them while awaiting other sisters and the superior, going back and forth between the two houses and keeping Mother Rosa informed of developments. The Mother chooses Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi as superior, who arrives in the first ten days of November. But further revelations emerge. The management runs at a loss, is costly and very demanding and burdensome financially as well. The atmosphere is difficult, not only because of the girls, often violent and quarrelsome, but also because of the constant and exacting supervision of the ladies of the Pious Union, who share responsibility for running the work with the director, Fr Bennicelli. On 27.11.1878 Mother Rosa sends him a letter setting everything out precisely (L 190). In conscience she cannot burden the Institute, which lives almost on Providence, with a financial liability. At most she can leave the sisters in the House on the same terms as the Josephite Sisters, i.e. £ 600 a year without any administrative responsibility. In fact three sisters remain with the superior. Meanwhile the Director sets about finding another religious Congregation to take over his work, and succeeds. On 25.12.1878 superior Illuminata reports to Mother Rosa a thorough inspection of every part of the "Pious House" by some foreign Sisters. Around Christmas the Mother therefore withdrew the superior, Sr. A. del Salvatore. Pending developments the community is entrusted to Sr. A. Eugenia Gaudenzi. In March Fr Bennicelli informs the Daughters of Saint Anne that they are released from all obligations, and so, having duly handed over, they leave the House on 23 March 1879.

Cf. AFSA. Rome - House for Penitent Women. D. 2. 12, F. 6. 46.

10. CERCOLA (Naples). Parish service - Orphanage - School

Among the many requests for sisters that reached Mother Rosa from Naples and its surroundings in 1878, the one from Cercola was considered above all others "a sign of divine providence. The offer could not be finer... It seems Saint Anne has chosen that place". So Mgr Filippo D'Amico wrote to M. Rosa when presenting the proposal on 30.6.1878. He had been approached by Comm. Domenico Riccardi, a wealthy landowner and mayor of Cercola, who, having "built a most beautiful church dedicated to the Immaculate Conception" with an adjoining "little convent" and cherishing a plan to benefit the poor of the town in some way, wanted the specific help of four Sisters, Daughters of Saint Anne. No less enthusiastic is superior Speranza Volpini: "this is truly a miracle of the Saint". By 27 September everything is ready, including the furnishing of the lodging for the sisters, completed thanks to superior Speranza's suggestions. The Commendatore then makes a formal request to the Foundress, specifying the sisters' roles: "... one who can play the organ, two who know something of medicine and the fourth experienced in surgery, to care for the sick of the Town. If the proposal is accepted, the Sisters should be in Cercola by 15.10.1878". Punctually on the appointed day Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, superior and organist, Sr. A. Potamiena Valcheresi, Sr. A. Zaveria Mangazzi and Sr. A. Faustina Battani are there, accompanied by Sup. Speranza Volpini. The next day the work is inaugurated with the sisters' official installation; from the 17th to the 22nd there are great popular festivities in the town for the consecration of the church and the Archbishop's visit. The sisters' specific task: the church, entirely in their care, from cleaning and the upkeep of the sacristy furnishings to the liturgy enlivened with singing and organ accompaniment. Services, more or less solemn, follow one another frequently through devotional months, novenas, triduums, feasts and liturgical seasons. The superior, an accomplished organist, must among other things teach the sisters the hymns and sing herself. On Sundays they help the chaplain with catechesis. "Here," she notes with fine humour, "we have to be priest, deacon, sacristan, etc.". To her far from light duties in the church Sr. A. Zaveria must add nursing the many poor sick who come to the house every day to receive medicines for their ailments or to have an aching, troublesome tooth pulled. There is also a hot meal to prepare for anyone in special need, and requests for home visits to patients unable to come to the sisters for the right medicine. Signora Antonietta, the Commendatore's wife, considers it almost her right as mistress to order sacred vestments to be sewn and embroidered for the church, and commissions items of linen for herself from the good sisters. She also entrusts her two little nieces to the cultured superior for lessons. In short, there is no lack of work, the superior writes to the Mother, keeping her informed of how the work is going and receiving encouragement and tokens of affection and approval (L 171; 214; 268; 298, etc.): "My dear daughter is all Jesus' and for Him she wants to live and die and toil" (L 237). Visiting the Cercola house at the end of January 1878, M. Rosa was confirmed in her excellent opinion of the work. She knows she can count on the abilities of the superior and the sisters. 1883 marks a turning point for the "little convent" with the start of, and turn towards, educational work. The orphanage is born as the Church's response to a tragic event: the earthquake that devastated Casamicciola on 29.7.1883. In the urgent relief work Archbishop Guglielmo Sanfelice mobilises the Church's resources and creates places and means of relief. To the Daughters of Saint Anne at Cercola he entrusts three little orphans, that they may be mothers and educators to them. Comm. Riccardi too opens his heart to charity, taking in ten and providing a small monthly allowance and premises next to the Sisters' lodging. It is also planned to benefit day girls by admitting them to the boarders' school, and a fee-paying boarding school for the "well-to-do" is projected. A fifth Sister with a teaching certificate gives the pupils their schooling, validated at the end of the year by examinations at the state elementary school. Embroidery, sewing and, for those who wish, piano complete the girls' formation, preparing them for an honourable and dignified future. After 1900 schools of every level are gradually established, up to a Teacher Training Institute. In 1930 the Postulancy opens, in 1932 the Novitiate, in 1953 the Aspirancy. It is still an important centre for compulsory-level schooling and for pastoral activity in the local church.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Cercola. F. 5. 37.

11. FAETO (Foggia). Municipal Nursery School

The opening of the Faeto house follows the usual procedure, as the Reg. Prot. 1876-1881 shows. On 31.8.1878 School Inspector Pasquale Benedetto asks for three sisters and sets out the administrative conditions. The Mother accepts; clarifications follow, the forwarding of qualifications for the decision of the Town Commission, the date of arrival and travel expenses for the three Sisters. The superior and head of the Infant School, Sr. A. Gasparina Baggini, the teacher Sr. A. Leopoldina Farina and the assistant Sr. A. Sebastiana Clerici arrived at Faeto on 3.11.1878. Lodgings are ready for them: three little rooms above the Infant School, furnished with the bare essentials. By 25 November they are already busy with some ninety children. They will be for them and with them full-time every day: from

8 am to 5 pm in winter, from 5 am to 7 pm in summer, and they will be able to take only a short break instead of the summer holidays of the other Schools "of the Kingdom". The calendar, as can be seen, follows the rhythms and seasons of field work of the local people, whose main livelihood is farming. The sisters set to work and achieve miracles with their little ones, who give a good account of what they have learnt both to the inspectors and to the Commission presiding over the two half-yearly examinations of the school year. A setback soon arises in the little religious community: Sr. A. Leopoldina is not used to teaching small children. After a fortnight she leaves and is replaced by Sr. A. Maddalena Terzaghi, who arrives with a fourth Sister to help: Sr. A. Prudenziana Demartini. Time passes quietly, and at the final examinations at the end of the 1878-79 school year everyone — children, families, authorities — is very satisfied with the good results. The following year looked set to bring nothing new, although cleverly contrived rumours were circulating in the town against the "nuns" and their "religious" methods of education. Mayor Pasquale Izzo felt it his duty to clear them before their Mother General: "The exemplary conduct of the Daughters of Saint Anne, beyond all praise, spares me from saying with what zeal and charity they fulfil their task to the town's satisfaction. Let this assure Your Ladyship that the local authority, jealous of the dignity and rare virtues with which these worthy educators perform their duties, hastens to clear them before you of the criticisms and charges brought by slanderers". In reaffirming the excellent references of the religious, Parish Priest Fr Rocco Gallucci went on to expose the slanderers' aim plainly: "a handful of self-seekers of this sort, used to living at public expense, would like to remove them and put someone of their own in their place". The superior then keeps the Mother informed of the plots of the Church's "adversaries", i.e. the party that in the last elections of July 1880 had won three town councillors, including the school inspector. Seizing the opportunity and turning to his advantage the annual expiry of the contract between the town and the two religious in post, and being unable to remove them altogether, he had appointed the teacher Sr. A. Pompilia Corradini, who had replaced Terzaghi, and a new lay head, Signora Celestina Berlocchi (his sister-in-law), in place of the superior, on the grounds that, not being subject "to continual transfers at the will of the Superior General", she guaranteed continuity at the Infant School. This was a cunningly devised measure to remove the religious in practice, since, as everyone knew, they live in community. The Daughters of Saint Anne left Faeto towards the end of November 1881.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Faeto. D. 2. 13.

12. ACI S. ANTONIO (Catania).

Municipal Elementary School - Hospital

Mayor Vincenzo Puglisi's proposal of 17.5.1878 to Mother R. Gattorno to send three teachers for a girls' school was accepted with a change: two teachers and a third Sister without qualifications as assistant. The procedure thus begun was completed within four months with the submission of the necessary documents and, while awaiting the departure date, the Mother kept the Sisters destined for Aci S. Antonio and Aci Catena ready by sending them to Naples, where they arrived on 14.10.1878; but the order to leave was given by the Mother only on 19.11.1878, as appears from Superior Tommasina Viterbo's account of the journey to the Mother. That same evening she sailed with Sr. A. Mattia Viterbo (the teacher) and Sr. A. Pudenziana, but their steamer collided with a boat and had to return to port and leave the following evening; this did not upset arrangements with the Mayor, who had organised the Sisters' welcome well, because on reaching Messina the Superior telegraphed him. At Acireale station they found two carriages waiting and representatives of the authorities — the Bishop's Vicar and the Aci S. Antonio town councillor — who took them to the Bishop, Mgr Gerlando M. Genuardi. Heartened by his fatherly kindness, they set off "most consoled" and in less than an hour reached their destination, where "priests and gentlemen" were waiting; all gave them the honours of "an extraordinary welcome, better than any other place I have been so far".

So wrote the Superior. It was 21.11.1878. The school opened on the 25th with two courses: the municipal school, with some seventy girls, entrusted to Sr. A. Mattia, and the private school, housed in the "College of Mary" (granted to the Sisters as their lodging), for girls of "civil", i.e. middle-class, families, assigned to the Superior, pending the planned construction of the Infant School (Nursery). The Mayor closely followed the progress of the school. He had received excellent references about the FSA, who at Agrigento were giving proof of fine organisational, teaching and educational ability. He therefore hoped for their valuable help in his efforts to open his town — "too old-fashioned", as the Superior had immediately noticed too — to the mainland culture of united Italy. He personally handled correspondence with the Superior General about the teaching staff. For the 1879-80 school year he asked her for a Sister to teach piano and expressed his satisfaction at the school's growth. The Daughters of Saint Anne found an open and fruitful field in forming the town's young women, and goodwill among their families. The girls attending school at the "College of Mary", founded in 1844 by its present director and administrator, the curate Francesco Di Grazia, though not strictly boarders, were bound to observe a rule of life outside school as well, including catechism, talks and regular reception of the sacraments. The College's long tradition had produced "good young women and good mothers of families". The Sisters soon widened their work in the town by caring for the sick. Two of them, while belonging to the school community, were called to serve at the hospital, where in 1902 lodgings were prepared for them and they formed a community of their own. The school legislation of the Kingdom of Italy, extended to the Schools of Sicily, required among other things that teachers be hired through competitions based on qualifications, in which lay teachers naturally took part as well. This brought binding obligations: valid qualifications, references, continuity in teaching, so that the school authorities met the frequent transfers of teachers ordered by M. Rosa with prohibitions and protests. There was also resentment and discontent among secular teachers who were sometimes passed over in favour of a Sister. The Sisters and friends floated the idea of a private school, but it remained only some people's wish. In 1914 a "Vocational Work School" was set up at the College of Mary, with a workshop making clothes and embroidery for sale. The Sisters worked in it for several years, but since it proved impossible to provide Sisters properly qualified at one of the Kingdom's Women's Vocational Schools (which existed only in Rome and Turin), in 1921 Mother General Sr. A. Celsa Speranza thought it best to withdraw the Sisters from the College and the hospital.

Cf. AFSA, Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Aci S. A.-D. 2. 13.

13. ACI CATENA (Catania). Orphanage - Municipal Elementary School

On 17.1.1878 the Bishop of Acireale, Mgr Gerlando Maria Genuardi, wrote to M. Rosa: "As I am opening at Aci Catena, a town bordering this episcopal city, a charitable house for the education of girls, I have thought of entrusting it to the diligent care of the Daughters of Saint Anne"; he explained that the house was entirely under his authority, as the "pious founder" had so stipulated, and added that for the present, besides educating the orphans, a school and a workshop for day girls could be opened, in the hope of later taking in little orphans as free boarders. The new house's funds could support three sisters. If she agreed, he asked her to come herself or send someone to visit the place, at his expense. M. Rosa sent Sr. A. Santina Solenghi and Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti to Acireale; the Bishop explained to them his plan for the present and the future developments of the work and invited them to go to Aci Catena with two Canons to inspect the premises and suggest suitable criteria for a practical renovation of the building and the furnishing of the rooms. The contract, approved and signed beforehand by the Mother, was concluded and, in view of how long the alterations would take, the Sisters' arrival was set for no earlier than November. For the time being, the Bishop said, their number must be limited to three; later, trusting in the protection of St Joseph, patron of the Church attached to the work, he hoped to increase it. On 1 December 1878 the first three FSA arrived: Sr. A. Federica Anfossi, Superior, Sr. A. Fausta Torriani for the school, Sr. A. Beata Torriani for the kitchen. In her report to the Mother (8.12.1878) the Superior dwells on the honourable welcome at Acireale station and the visit to the Bishop, who received them very kindly and blessed them, happy to open an FSA house in his Diocese. On reaching the seat of the work, called the "Conservatory of Virgins", they found the door open and inside, waiting, "the whole Town Council, the Superintendent and two priests". But a surprise awaited them "at once": "a councillor comes in accompanied by 10 girls (the orphan boarders) and behind them eight nuns". Who these were the Mayor explained on his next visit: "girls of the college who, having passed the age limit and not wishing to leave, have dressed as nuns. The eldest has become their superior and another their teacher". For reasons of charity and good order, since the older residents had adopted a way of life according to their own habits and choices, it was agreed that they needed to be separated in a part of the house of their own, making the two communities independent. The town at first regarded the "Italian Sisters" with some indifference, but on getting to know them began to show esteem and veneration. After the examinations the Mother received excellent reports: "the Conservatory is making great progress... the teacher Torriani and her pupils have earned the warmest praise". So wrote Canon Giuseppe Bella to M. Rosa on 16 August; the Bishop had appointed him to represent him in running the orphanage, and he was also the Sisters' confessor. In the following years Mother Rosa sent two more sister teachers, strengthening the municipal school, which was held in the same premises as the "Conservatory"; one of them was given the mixed class of the municipal school in the S. Filippo district. At the end of the 1881-82 school year the Mother thought it best to transfer three Sisters from the school but, as the papers of their replacements were not submitted in time, the provincial school authorities replaced them with lay staff. This was due not only to hostility towards the religious but also to considerations of fairness: many lay women with proper teaching qualifications were pressing for work. Only the two Sisters at the orphanage were confirmed in post. But the Mother thought it best to withdraw them.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundation - Aci C. D. 2. 13.

14. LA PAZ - BOLIVIA.

"St John of God" and "Loaiza" Hospitals

The departure of the first group of FSA for Bolivia is the historic response to the missionary charism that the Foundress felt and instilled in her followers — a response given by the whole Family. Mother Rosa in fact asked all the communities that "whoever" felt called to "go to America" should say so (L 124). From among the many she then chose and prepared the 16 who in her judgement met the requirements: Sr. A. Cunegonda Conti, Sr. A. Felicita Conti, Sr. A. Livia Tallarini, Sr. A. Modesta Molesti, Sr. A. Zoila Levi, Sr. A. Amodio Gregori, Sr. A. Perpetua Torrielli, Sr. A. Annunciata Chiodelli, Sr. A. Lucia Taraballi, Sr. A. Clelia Semeria, Sr. A. Damiana Giovenetti, Sr. A. Gaudiosa Scandolari, Sr. A. Domitilla Solenghi,

Sr. A. Scolastica Barelliani, Sr. A. Bonaventura Tornelli, Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, Superior. With arrangements finalised with Fr Vincenzo Rocchi (L 144; 148; 150), the "fine" band leaves Piacenza on 22 November 1878 and, accompanied by the same Father, sails from Genoa the next day (L 186). The journey is long and exhausting. They finally reach La Paz on 20 January 1879, welcomed with honour by the highest religious and civil Authorities and by the people. Amid general jubilation, ovations, showers of flowers, ringing of bells and music from the town band, they pass through streets decked out for the feast with triumphal arches, flags and hangings from balconies and windows, and are escorted to the church of the "Recoleta", beside the College of Propaganda Fide, seat of the Franciscan Fathers, for the singing of the Te Deum; then to the Town Hall for the official speeches of welcome, and finally to the house of the Bishop's brother, Don Benigno Clavijo, who with his wife feels honoured to host them, as their lodgings at the hospital are not ready. At last they can rest. They are dazed and amazed at such an unexpected welcome, but one more surprise moves them: the Mother has gone ahead of them with a letter. Her words sink into their hearts, a balm of consolation, full of optimism and courage for the new adventure (L 207).

The official inauguration and "handing over" of the two hospitals to the religious was set for 1 February, but no one had bothered to prepare suitable lodgings for them in either. A hall of the "S. Juan" is then hastily adapted by moving the patients elsewhere, without, however, having it properly disinfected. As a result some Sisters contract typhus, which on the 28th of that month carries Sr. A. Scolastica Barelliani to the grave and on 6 March Sr. A. Modesta Molesti. The contagion goes on striking one after another. The Town Council steps in with the timely measure of releasing the Sisters from hospital service and moving them elsewhere. The sick are housed and nursed until fully recovered by families belonging to the "Charitable Society". The Mother, unaware of this harsh reality, keeps writing for news. Only in May does word of the two Sisters' deaths reach her (L 291). The other seven who fell ill have recovered, but reinforcements are needed, so the benefactor Don Benigno Clavijo has promised to pay the journey of ten more Sisters, whom Fr Rocchi will accompany as he did the first.

Many young Bolivian women wish to be received as postulants. The Mother is heartened by the work's happy start and takes the steps needed to meet the needs for staff and facilities, above all the erection of the Novitiate. But the first consoling news is followed by months of inexplicable silence that grows ever more painful (L 299; 311; 328; 357; 369). The mystery will be solved in October, when she can hold in her hands the shaky handwriting of her Giuseppa, who "by a miracle of God" has come through, after three months, a severe bout of spotted typhus and its complications.

Now all have recovered. Only four Sisters came through the trial unscathed. They resume service at the hospital and in a short time transform and put everything in order, sparing no effort in cleaning and organising the two hospitals. With admirable self-denial and sacrifice they personally disinfect and rid the wards of vermin thoroughly.

So begins in the two large hospitals of La Paz (each with 250 beds) the mission of the Daughters of Saint Anne, "las heroinas de la caridad", whose memory will live on for generations. But the reach of their charity extends to other fields.

In the "Bolivian Red Cross". When the "War of the Pacific" broke out between Bolivia and Peru on one side and Chile on the other, the Sisters, under the direction of Bishop Mgr Juan de Dios Bosque, organised everything needed to care for the wounded and made thousands of scapulars of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, which they handed to the soldiers with their own hands (letter of Sup. Giuseppa to M. Rosa: 14.9.1879). Later they would go as far as Tacna to nurse the wounded and see to their transport to La Paz.

They also take over the hospital pharmacy. Sr. A. Annunciata Chiodelli, after obtaining the qualification to complete the Italian certificates sent by M. Rosa (L 425; 437), is in charge of it. Meanwhile requests for the Sisters arrive from the hospitals of Sucre, the Capital, and Potosí (L 408).

The field is truly immense. In education a School is opened; then comes the erection of the Novitiate, promising wider horizons.

Cf. AFSA. Foundations Bolivia, La Paz. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. F. 3. 26.

15. CROTONE. Orphanage - Elementary School

M. Rosa's acceptance of the proposal made to her by the Bishop on 9.11.1878 rekindled in him and in all those keen to reopen the orphanage, closed for three years, the hope of reviving a highly humanitarian work for poor girls struck by misfortune. It had been established as a Charitable Foundation in 1841 by Baron Pietro Belingeri and entrusted to lay staff, but had closed because of various difficulties. Only a religious Congregation could revive it, and providence made use of the FSA. Three arrived late in the evening of 26.2.1879. Welcomed by two women who offered them coffee and a cake, after a quick tour of the "convent" they retired to their longed-for rest. Next day Superior Sr. A. Elisa Corsini, Sr. A. Beatrice Merici and Sr. A. Nemisia Orlandi are at work. The administrator presents them to the Bishop and to the various Barons and Marquises, "the masters", who express confidence in their work. "They leave it to us to put in order this orphanage, always badly run and closed for three years". The 11 orphans supported by the "Commission" were to come in on 1 March, and later others, fee-paying. A day school was also wanted. Such was the news the Superior gave the Mother in her first letter of 28.2.1879, followed by reports on the progress of the community and the work. The place is gloomy: built like a "strictly enclosed monastery", in need of cleaning and of organisation in everything from kitchen to classrooms, dormitories and linen room. There is much work and the need for another Sister is soon evident. In May two arrive, so the day school can be started too. But poverty is always "at home" with the FSA. Months go by without the salary due. The Bishop apologises to the Superior and an attempt is made to remedy matters by renewing the administrative "Commission". The Sisters' dedication to forming their pupils is admirable and, seeing the good results, the "Charity Congregation" asks for two Sisters for the Infant School; it also wishes to entrust them with the girls' Elementary School.

The small original community was the fruitful seed of the other social services that sprang up within a few years in response to the town's needs: nursing at the hospital (1879), the foundling home (1881), two Nursery Schools and two Elementary Schools, one of which, the "S. Cuore School", is still running.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Crotone. D. 3. 19.

16. S. GIOVANNI DI BELLAGIO (Como). Nursery School

When the lay teacher of the Nursery School was no longer available, the parish priest, Archpriest Domenico Bolzani, thought it advisable to entrust it to two Sisters. He wrote to the Bishop of Piacenza setting out the advantages the parish would gain from the presence of the religious, who could also help him as catechists and leaders of the Sunday oratory for girls and visit the sick at home when needed. Having obtained support, he sent his request to Mother Rosa Gattorno, but was told that two Sisters were impossible: three at least. The Commission running the Infant School met and agreed to accept three, with an annual allowance of £ 1,100 besides free furnished premises; income allowed no higher payment. Informed of the decision, the Mother asked Bishop Mgr Pietro Carsana for permission and his blessing, and then prepared the Sisters: Sr. A. Fiorenza Riboldi, Superior, Sr. A. Amelia Lari, Sr. A. Sofia Mazzinghi. The archpriest himself went to fetch them from Piacenza, and they arrived at Bellagio on 17.7.1879.

The joyful welcome of the whole population repaid the three Sisters for the discomforts of the journey. At the entrance to the "most beautiful villa" a swarm of noisy children with drums and little flags, accompanied by a priest; the road to the parish crowded with good country folk who had come to greet them, and the Church just as packed (cf. L Sr. A. Fiorenza Riboldi).

The house fills with children and young people; 60 little ones attend regularly. Every Sunday there is school for young women who want to learn or practise reading and writing. Catechism takes up a good deal of time, as does the singing school. Towards the end of the year a fourth sister, Stefania Margotti, joined them to help the others; she will be wholly supported by the Institute.

On 20 December 1880 the parish priest thanks the Mother "for the good the Sisters do the parish by their teaching and good example" and says he trusts in providence to sustain the "pious institution".

Some years later, again expressing his gratitude, he regrets being unable to help them as they deserve and "leaving them in such privation". The members of the Commission, chaired by Duke Melzi with the parish priest Bolzani as vice-chairman, were understanding, esteemed them and were keen to keep the four Daughters of Saint Anne. With the next vice-chairman, Archpriest Tomaso Verga, there was some friction over expenses the Superior had incurred for the Infant School, which he considered unnecessary. In 1897 an agreement was drawn up to confirm the terms set from the beginning and, to the great satisfaction of the townspeople, deeply attached to the Sisters, the work went on for years more, at no small sacrifice. In August 1903 Mother Benedetta Carrega, in view of the local administration's financial difficulties and the Sisters' privations, thought it best to withdraw them.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Bellagio. D. 2. 15.

17. LA PAZ - BOLIVIA. Saint Anne School

The first agreement between M. Rosa Gattorno and Fr Vincenzo Rocchi provided for opening one or more "educational establishments", so the Mother added two teachers to the sister nurses. A school was already in view because of the many requests from families. Sr. A. Scolastica Barelliani and Sr. A. Modesta Molesti were to have been the "pioneers" in Bolivian schooling. But death took them at the young ages of 29 and 31, cutting short the hopes of those who already saw them engaged in the vitally important mission of the all-round formation of women, until then almost entirely neglected even in La Paz, though it was the most important city in Bolivia. Superior Giuseppa wrote to the Mother on 15.5.1879: "we have not had the consolation of starting the school, though there were many girls who wanted to come; God has willed it so". A private school run by a single teacher, Miss Clara Telleria, was operating, modest in size but excellent in aims and results. This was the seed of the School opened by the Daughters of Saint Anne, who joined forces with this worthy teacher; having come to know the Sisters at the hospital, she had wished to follow them and had received the habit on 30.8.1879, taking the name Sr. A. Rosa (L 389).

The school opens on 10 September 1879 with Sr. A. Damiana Giovenetti for academic subjects and Sr. A. Livia Tallerini for needlework. They are joined by the novice Sr. A. Rosa Telleria, very dear to the Foundress, who corresponded with her (L 408; 425; 435) and some years later, when she fell ill, allowed her to go to Piacenza, where sadly she died on 5.8.1884. At first it has 84 girls and receives a small monthly grant from the "Municipality". It is kept going with difficulty and sacrifice for several years. In 1892 the Superior, Sr. A. Virginia Gaggi, obtains government authorisation for the primary school, with the obligation to conform to state rules and regulations. From then on, thanks to the untiring, precious help of influential people, parents and all who value the teaching of the

Sisters, the School is consolidated and developed, gaining a full range of courses, a large boarding section and spacious premises equipped for its various academic and extracurricular activities.

The "Colegio Santa Ana" is still a prestigious and effective institution for the cultural and formative service it offers new generations.

Cf. AFSA. E 2. 13. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Bolivia.

18. BELLINZAGO - (Novara). "De Medici" Infant School

The School founded by the lawyer Gabriele De Medici and built to a design by the well-known architect Alessandro Antonelli was inaugurated on 28.5.1876 and entrusted by the administrative Commission to the Sisters of St Aloysius for direction and teaching. When the three-year term expired the contract was terminated. They turned to M. Rosa Gattorno, who reached agreement by letter with the parish priest, Fr Pietro Paolo Ottone, a member of the Commission. The first four Sisters were to arrive on 6 October, followed by two more for the regular opening set for the 15th of that month. The first Superior and head is Sr. A. Veneranda Picco. With her are Sr. A. Ester Scagliarini, Sr. A. Daria Negri, Sr. A. Nestore Tagliabue and Sr. A. Ermelinda (?). A few days later Sr. A. Gesualda Polenghi and Sr. A. Modestina Bottini arrive. The building is new, beautiful and imposing, the rooms spacious. The chapel, however, lacks everything. The Superior informs the Mother on every aspect: the house and its surroundings, relations with the authorities, the organisation of the school and the community. She asks her for chapel furnishings, teaching books and whatever else the Sisters need. She is short of money because the salary is paid at the end of the month. The Mother helps, advises (L 411; 415; 429; 441) and buys for the chapel a chalice, a pyx, candlesticks, an altar cloth and flower vases.

At first the school has 300 pupils, but the Sisters extend their educational service to girls of 13 to 15 with private lessons and also teach catechism. Six months after the opening the Education Officer of Novara visits and is pleased with the good results and the Sisters' teaching and educational skills. The Superior-head and the Sisters carry out their mission with dedication, joyful simplicity and kindness, never tired of spending themselves for the children who overcrowd their classrooms, and for young people and families. When in 1905 Mother General Benedetta Carrega decided to transfer Sr. A. Veneranda, a unanimous chorus of praise rose for her and the Sisters: "if this Infant School has risen to such prosperity as to rank among the best in the district, it is certainly due also to the good management and beneficial work of the worthy FSA".

The Sisters still carry on their educational and pastoral mission in the school and the oratory, loved and esteemed by pupils, parents and townspeople, fully integrated into and sharing in the life of the parish community.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Bellinzago. E 5. 38.

19. BEVAGNA (Perugia). "Bartolini" Orphanage

On 20 January 1879 the Superior of the Foligno House, Sr. A. Guglielma Merli, at the invitation of Fr Giuseppe Bartolini, goes to Bevagna to visit the orphanage he has decided to found in his native town for poor girls. She writes to the Mother, convinced of the work's usefulness and likely success, praising the administrator, Fr Giuseppe, "a person all charity and kindness, God-fearing". The Mother is pleased with the good news and will make arrangements directly with him when he writes to her (L 244). The Father begins a correspondence with her and they finally reach agreement on the number of Sisters, three at least, and their duties in the orphanage, which would start with nine girls and was expected to grow, as well as on their remuneration and the date of the inauguration. Mother Rosa chooses the Sisters in agreement with the Superior of Foligno; the Father fetches them there on 15.10.1879, and together with that Superior, who will stay with them three days, Sr. A. Edvige Santori, Sr. A. Linda Dughi and Sr. A. Ubaldina Cavacciuti, Superior, set out. A group of Ladies gives them a warm welcome, and the newcomers are delighted with the well-furnished, well-stocked house.

According to the founder's regulations the orphanage takes in seven girls up to the age of 18 and provides for their all-round formation. They are given basic religious and general education and trained in weaving. Fr Giuseppe directed it until his death in 1900, after which the Bartolini family kept up its interest, as he had left the task to an heir among his brothers.

Over the years the number of residents was raised to 16 and their formation was strengthened, with good results, by courses of primary schooling and home economics, besides specialist training in weaving.

The Sisters' community was withdrawn for lack of staff in January 1962, after more than 80 years of "generous dedication and motherly charity", as one of the Bartolini heirs attests.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Bevagna. D. 2. 17.

20. COSENZA. School - Boarding School

On 7.2.1879 Fr Agostino Donadio wrote from Cosenza to M. Rosa Gattorno: "I am working to bring your daughters here; the Archbishop would be delighted. Here hospital, poorhouse, orphanage, schools — everything is in the hands of secular persons and everyone is tired of it. What is most wanted is an educational Institute for girls of good family, which is lacking, so families are obliged to send their daughters to Naples... everyone says they want the Daughters of Saint Anne. There are only two enclosed monasteries; sisters of charity have not yet come here, so it will be a fine stroke if we can establish your daughters here... We would begin with the boarding school". M. Rosa replies gratefully, accepts and supports his initiative (L 259), and within a month the Father can tell her the matter is settled. He has found lodgings for the Sisters in a palazzo in piazza Polleri belonging to the Ronchi Ladies, who want to do some good. The Parish Priest of the Cathedral, Canon Raffaele Parise, undertakes to the Archbishop to furnish the premises made available to the Sisters and to provide for their upkeep (L Fr Agostino to M. Rosa: 23.2.1879).

At this point Canon Parise forwards to the Foundress a request for three Sisters to educate the orphans. On receiving a favourable answer, negotiations proceed and both sides prepare what is needed. On 24 October 1879, the agreed date, four Sisters are in place: Sr. A. Vincenza Tornatore, Superior, Sr. A. Crescenzia Tarantino, Sr. A. Bibiana Bersagli, Sr. A. Germana Cammelli. But their first impression is a disappointment. Instead of the large premises held out by good Fr Agostino (palazzo indeed!!) they find only two rooms for the school, one bedroom for the Sisters, a dark little room and the kitchen. Sr. A. Vincenza pours out her heart to the Mother, who encourages her: "I am happier this way, because after the storms the sky clears.

The Bishop (Mgr Camillo Sorgente) has written me many fine things; he tells me he will help you and be a father to you" (L 403).

People are pleased at their arrival. On 4 November the school opens with about 20 girls. Parish Priest Parise plans to open the boarding school in a "little flat" next to the Sisters' lodging, to be rented, and in fact at the start of the new school year the boarding school opens with five girls of "good" family, with others in view. They are given an education suited to their station: besides the school subjects, lessons in piano, French and embroidery. The number of day pupils grows, but the work cannot develop because space is rather cramped. It is hoped that in time the Ronchi ladies, besides the few rooms made available to the Sisters, will bequeath the whole palazzo. Things go on like this for a decade.

In July 1889 Superior Gonzaga Boeri informs the Mother of an excellent opportunity: the Daughters of Charity, whom Parish Priest Parise had called to run a boarding school and school, are withdrawing, thus vacating the spacious and practical house he had had built for the purpose; he proposes merging the two works and entrusting them to the Daughters of Saint Anne. The agreement is signed on 4 October 1889.

The boarding school takes in middle-class girls for a fee and girls of the people free of charge. Attached are the school and a workshop which, run by a needlework mistress, will serve not only for training but also for making and selling finely embroidered items.

As Fr Agostino had foreseen, the Daughters of Saint Anne were called to other areas of social welfare. The "Administration of Public Welfare Establishments" entrusted them with the direction of the orphanage under a regular contract in 1887 and with the hospital in 1889.

Other communities were opened after M. Rosa's death. The Educational and Welfare Institute and the hospital are still in operation.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Cosenza. F 5. 37, B. 5. 97.

21. LINGUAGLOSSA (Catania). Municipal Elementary School

The Town Council, having decided to entrust the direction and teaching of the municipal girls' school to religious teachers,

turned, on the advice of the Bishop of Acireale, to the Foundress of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

The Mayor submitted the request on 29.7.1879. Two Sisters with "lower grade" certificates (to teach the first cycle) were needed. On 3 August the Mother answered yes, provided there were at least three Sisters.

Negotiations concluded with the Town providing free lodging and an annual salary of £ 500 for three Sisters, one with a higher-grade and two with lower-grade certificates; a fourth was accepted as assistant. Five arrived in the first ten days of November 1879: Sr. A. Speciosa Fortini, Sr. A. Generosa Borgiani and Sr. A. Onorina Astolfi, teachers, Sr. A. Ermenegilda to help, and Sr. A. Desideria Aliprandi, superior. They had, however, to make do with temporary lodgings. Writing to the Mother on 14.11.1879 the Superior says among other things: "they did not receive us with a band, but I found kindness in all the authorities, ecclesiastical and civil". The Mother asks the Superior of the Agrigento house, Sr. A. Domenica Schenardi, to visit the new work and receives reassuring reports from her. The Mayor had regretted the Sisters' early arrival but had immediately found makeshift but comfortable premises: "they have everything they need, the classrooms well equipped, there is a kitchen, a refectory and enough room to sleep. There is no chapel, but the Church is near. They will have to make sacrifices for a year, until the conversion of the former convent of the Dominican Fathers, handed over to the Town after the suppression of ecclesiastical property, is completed".

In the same month the Sisters arrived (November 1879), the President of the Charity Congregation, in agreement with the Mayor, proposes to the Mother that one of the five Sisters be assigned to nurse the patients of the "S. Rocco" hospital and suggests, to get round the objection raised by the local Superior regarding the Rule's prohibition, detaching a second Sister from the school community — the one in charge of household tasks — and replacing her with a lay woman. The hospital could not afford to hire other staff. No solution was found then other than the one suggested by the Mother: the Superior could be present at the hospital by visiting the sick during the week.

The school opens its doors with 70 pupils in the three lower classes, and catechism is taught in the church as the Bishop wished. The school grows rapidly and the teachers do themselves credit, so much so that when the Mother wants to transfer one, the authorities and families put up strong resistance.

Inspired by the spirit of motherly self-giving proper to the Congregation, the Sisters did not neglect the town's educational needs or the requests for help from families and, faithful to the style of poverty M. Rosa kept to in her practical choices, later opened a small boarding school, a private nursery and elementary school and a needlework school, which in time grew in numbers and effectiveness.

In 1886 the FSA took up their permanent mission at the hospital and kept it until 1949.

After 1900, as lay teachers increased, the Sisters withdrew from the municipal School, while continuing their other works.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Linguaglossa. D. 3. 20.

22. CROTONE. Hospital

The Daughters of Saint Anne had been at Crotone a few months when the Mother was asked for their service to the patients of the small, poor hospital, for which two Sisters were thought sufficient. She replied that she would accept only by sending three, as the Rules required.

Agreement was reached, since both sides had the patients' welfare at heart. The Administration would give the three religious a salary of fr 70 a month, lodging and travel.

Sr. A. Ausiliatrice Besso, Superior, Sr. A. Mistica Limongi and Sr. A. Amadio Gilberti arrive on 29.12.1879. Within a few days they put things in order and clean thoroughly, starting with the beds "full of insects". "We have so much work," the Superior writes on 3 January 1880, "that we can do no more". The patients are cared for with diligence and charity, and their number soon rises from 11 to 18; the President and the Commission are satisfied, "so much so that they invite visitors" to see the unexpected transformation, a prelude to future improvements.

Over the years the hospital gains a reputation. Services increase, and facilities and the number of beds are expanded. The number of Sisters grows too: 5 in 1892, 11 in 1934. FSA have followed one another for over a century, to this day, devoted to the sick in a hospital complex that is constantly being modernised. At present two are engaged in hospital chaplaincy.

Cf. AFSA. Reg. Prot. 1876-1881. Foundations - Crotone. D. 3. 19.
