PRESENTATION

It is a gift for the whole Family of Saint Anne and for all who wish to know Mother Rosa Gattorno to be able to come into contact with another volume of her letters, in the very year in which, by a providential coincidence, we celebrate the centenary of her birth into heaven and, with deeper joy in communion with the whole Church, the event of her Beatification.

How can we thank the good God, who has granted us this grace, so long awaited by our religious Family, at such significant times?

This interweaving of events in the Holy Year draws us more intensely into the attitude of conversion so characteristic of Mother Rosa, and brings us closer to her teaching.

In this volume the Mother shows herself a creature wholly dependent on her Crucified Good, intent solely on becoming one with Him and on forming her spiritual daughters to live grounded in His own values.

She is constantly concerned to steep them in the spirit of the charism she bears, with motherly exhortations touching the essentials of life and of the process of transformation in Christ Jesus.

She shares with them the hopes and labours involved in developing the Work God entrusted to her.

Her labours do not check her apostolic zeal and her love for the Work, which she sees growing with new vocations through the providential support of God, whose faithfulness she experiences.

The letters of this period reveal faith, toil and tenacity in carrying out a mission of many charitable facets.

Her apostolic drive, as she moves forward to consolidate the foundations of the Work, clearly portrays a woman of faith and unconditional charity, able to hope against all hope.

Between the lines of the letters one sees that the Work's expansion demands of her time, energy and great effort in forming future religious in the Institute's distinctive identity and in professional skill, to meet the different areas of the mission: pastoral, educational, nursing and social-educational.

5

Yet overwork does not distract her from living in God, so that she radiates strength of spirit and apostolic energy.

She forms the Sisters in this way of life, encouraging them to develop a spirit of service and obedience so as to live their mission faithfully as true daughters of Holy Mother Anne.

She constantly calls them to recognise the divine mercies received from God, especially that of being recognised in the Church as Daughters of Saint Anne (cf. Lett. 24).

The Mother was firmly convinced that the Work belonged to her dear Crucified One; so she took upon herself the sufferings its growth entailed, living with humility and charity the disagreements with a Dicastery of the Church over the approval of the Constitutions.

Yet with transparency and filial trust she patiently and simply set out the truth of the facts.

Growing perfect in the school of suffering, she came to repeat to her daughters too: "whoever cannot suffer cannot love"; "courage, it is a time of trials, but Jesus is with us"; "courage, daughter, only in trials do the works of the Lord grow" (Lett. 497, 259).

She becomes a teacher in the school of suffering, whose only reason is to share her sorrows with Jesus, cooperating in what was "lacking in his passion" for the salvation of humanity, and finding comfort, strength and courage in Him alone.

May the letters in this volume call all members of the Family of Saint Anne, founded by Mother Rosa Gattorno, to carry out their mission with trust in the Father of eternal mercy, in the now approaching Third Millennium.

The words addressed to the recipients of these letters can be applied to today's readers too, as the words of a tender and beloved mother who continues to pass on her experience of affection and total surrender to the unconditional Love of the dear Crucified One.

Her advice and exhortations remain valid today in carrying out our mission on the various continents where we work as members of her Family.

Her great teachings on openness to the Spirit spur us to live, like her, in total abandonment, helping us grow in the tender fatherhood and motherhood so needed by people today.

As a Son of Saint Anne I cannot fail to express my joy at presenting this sixth volume of our dear Mother's letters, feeling myself too a recipient of the precious advice and teachings she passes on. Reading the letters to write this presentation, I was moved, for I felt myself the fruit of her openness to the voice of the Spirit, to the call of the mission "ad gentes" and to the inspiration to found the Institute of the "Sons of Saint Anne", as she herself attests in her Memoirs: "How I feel the need to have the Sons of Saint Anne..., I see them full of love, evangelising the whole world and giving the Work of the Daughters a most beautiful lustre".

INTRODUCTION

The dynamism of growth

With its bundle of 507 letters, the two years 1880-'81 add further important pages to the history of the Institute's beginnings. We are still in the great exploratory and prophetic season of the origins — the fifteenth year of its life — and the charism is spreading in Italy and has reached abroad (Bolivia), entering with bursting vitality into the social and charitable institutions that met the urgent needs of the time.

A hundred postulants receive the religious habit in 1880, one hundred and thirty-nine in 1881; 26 houses are opened in the two years (cf. L 267 and the circular L of 1882, to be published). These significant figures point to the richness of an organism growing in both its human and its structural dimensions. The Mother welcomes the new members as gifts of the Heavenly Father, living stones for building "His Work". She cares for them and nourishes them with "her spirit", shaping in each one a woman capable of unconditional self-giving to God in the service of others. She provides for their education and, according to each one's abilities and aptitudes, has them obtain the qualifications and professional skills needed for the various services in the religious and welfare works whose direction she accepts in response to society's many requests. Her letters to her dear daughters remain today the most living and effective witness to her work as Mother and formator.

In dialogue with society

But there is another field open to the most varied and wide-ranging relations, those "ad extra" concerning the foundations already made and those under way. Incoming correspondence is almost entirely preserved in the Institute's Archive under the relevant headings. The replies, those of the Foundress, have been recovered only in small part. This gap is filled for these two years by the Institute's Protocol Register 1876-1881. The Mother personally kept the register in date order, noting the sender and a summary of each letter. The reply to requests for Sisters, with rare exceptions, is positive: "accepted", followed in the space provided by the type of service required (school, hospital, etc.).

The dynamism of charity led her to take on needs in the social-health and educational-welfare fields, as in previous years. With preferential attention to the poor, she was also present in emergency relief. During the famine of 1880, together with the Church of Piacenza, she and her Sisters prepared and distributed soup to the poor. In 1881 she enthusiastically took on the care of the infants, still at the breast, of the women working in the "Tobacco Factory" (L 324). These works were housed in two crèches (nursing rooms) attached to the factories in Rome and Chiaravalle (AN) (cf. Index IV, 14 and 25).

Each FSA community working in public or private institutions is governed by precise legal provisions in "agreements" or contracts for which she alone is the point of reference and responsible party. It falls to her to negotiate and resolve problems with the Administrations, the first and most delicate being the assignment and transfer of Sisters. It is for her to discern whether to accept a requested collaboration or withdraw the Sisters when their presence is no longer considered necessary, or for other reasons. In these two years she opened 26 houses but had to close 4 that had been running for some time. The Institute is also acquiring works of its own and buildings it owns.

This phase of expansion and consolidation is certainly neither easy nor painless. But the Mother does not lack courage and fortitude, nor the gifts of nature and grace with which God has endowed her for the mission entrusted to her. She can also count on her daughters. She loves them and goes before them, embracing them in her Crucified Good, and advances with them in the adventure of Love. "Nothing pleases our Beloved but to be loved. So we must try everything to make Him loved and served by the whole world" (L 274).

Mother Rosa Gattorno.

The Foundress's sufferings

The sacrificial dimension carries great weight throughout Mother Rosa's life. This appears also in the letters published here, in which she herself often strikes the note of suffering. One day (7 February 1881) she confided to her niece Sr. A. Francesca Savignone: "Listen, the crosses are multiplying. May God give me the strength to bear everything" (L 302).

She had learnt from her Crucified Good to take on "suffering" and transform it into the energy of love. "Whoever cannot suffer cannot love" was her maxim. In her letters to those she confided in, she filtered this "suffering" through the range of her feelings, colouring it with meaningful shades — sorrow, tribulation, bitterness, affliction, anguish, pain... — and so creating an empathetic sharing.

The causes of her suffering can be guessed if we bear in mind her sensitivity, the far from easy tasks she was called to carry out and the relationships that extended from the narrow circle of her own family to the most diverse realities.

A great sorrow for her in April 1881 was the death of one of her two little granddaughters, Rosetta, struck down by diphtheria. Informed of the epidemic while in Rome, she had vainly urged her daughter and son-in-law to remove them from the danger of infection. She arrived in time to save the other, taking her with her to Fiorenzuola (L 353).

Then there were the problems of the Sisters' illnesses and deaths (14 in 1880, 12 in 1881) and their replacement. Other sorrows came from the unexemplary behaviour of some daughters and its negative effects on the communities; also from the hostility of people outside the Institute, and disputes with some Administrations.

But the strongest and most lasting anguish came from the Church authorities. In 1881 the Mother went through a crucial period in her relations with the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars over a juridical problem concerning the Constitutions, to which, in that Congregation's judgement, additions and modifications {animadversiones) should have been made in a special General Chapter. This was held on 23 August under the chairmanship of the Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr Scalabrini. Having learnt the content of the animadversiones, the capitulars did not consider them useful or beneficial for the Institute and rejected a good part of them.

Consequently on 6 October the Mother was summoned to the Sacred Congregation to account for the acts of that Chapter (L 290 n. 2). She could not travel for health reasons. On 16 November the summons was repeated through Bishop Scalabrini. On 3 December she was received in audience. The capitulars' attitude, perhaps beyond their real intentions, was regarded by the Ecclesiastical Authorities as an act of grave insubordination, which naturally fell upon the Mother.

In the ensuing audience the Mother humbled herself, explained her views on questions vital to the Institute (L 482; 483; 484) and met with broad understanding.

The differences were resolved. Cardinal Protector Alimonda would take up the matter and prove an effective mediator.

Meanwhile another dispute arose with Fr Francesco Chemin over the House at Bassano del Grappa (cf. Index IV, 10).

The way of sorrows continues. But the Mother presses on uphill with the strength of her Crucified Good. "Courage, it is a time of trials, but Jesus is with us!" (L 497).

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Superior had written (L n.d.) that she would have liked to complain to the Parish Priest because he had not supported her request to the Mayor to raise the salary of the sister teachers at the Infant School.

2 The Infant School was going well and the Sisters were doing themselves credit.

3 The postulant arrived in Piacenza on 26.1.1880. Cf. Reg. Post. no. 712.

She urges her to look after her health. She has done everything well; she approves her decisions on the community, the hospital and the school. Advice about a Sister. She awaits payment for goods sent. She asks for news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours dated 10 November, which arrived here on 18 Jan. 1880. I hear you are still very weak; for pity's sake look after your health, which always worries me greatly; take care not to overtax yourself and take every imaginable precaution. Yes, I command it.1

  2. As regards the church you have done everything well;2 I approve all you do; go forward with courage and do not lose heart, for pity's sake. If gentle means fail, one must often resort to the rod — the Holy Spirit says so too;3 so take heart; I would not want you to be distressed; I repeat that as regards observance, do as you think best.

  3. Likewise with the contracts, go ahead; I leave you full freedom, knowing that you certainly do everything for the best.4

  4. Is it true that Sr. A. Lucia has died? For in one of yours you spoke of her being seriously ill and then left it there; I would like to know.5 I will write a couple of lines to Sr. A. Perpetua; she has always had that bad habit of wanting to stay praying or doing something else instead of her duty; I say bad because when we neglect our own duty, those prayers certainly cannot be acceptable to God! No! As for the school, you have done everything well.6

  5. I hope you receive my letter — I can say my letters, for I have already written you a good number, by every post; try to do the same. In the last one there was also one for Sr. A. Rosa.7

  6. If you knew how much I have to do, almost always alone, I can say. It is horribly cold here; there has been a tremendous frost for 47 days. Oh! If you saw it! Dear daughter, enough; there is such poverty!

  7. For pity's sake, see whether you can send me the 2000 F. for the case of goods I sent you, which cost me real effort; what can I do, he wants to be paid,8 and you will understand that it is no small sum; I hope you will send it.

  8. Listen, is it true that that good president of the republic has been removed, is it true?9 Oh, I was truly sorry; and what is the one they have elected like? Let us hope the Saint makes him all goodness towards you. I greet you all, and you in particular, and call myself for all ages,

affectionate M. Rosa

Onorata greets you and asks you to send her a little monkey.

1 Sr. A. Giuseppa was still feeling the effects of her very serious illness, from May to August 1879, from which she had been saved by a miracle.

2 She had decided to have community prayers said in a small chapel set up in the hospital, going afterwards to the church for Mass.

3 She quotes freely: Sir 30:1 "whoever loves his son uses the rod, so as to rejoice in him at the end" and Proverbs 23:13 "do not withhold correction from a youth".

4 As regards the contracts, she had been advised to review the one agreed in Piacenza between Fr Rocchi and the Mother so as to improve it in the Institute's favour.

5 Sr. A. Lucia Taraballi had died on 14.9.'79 of typhus, which carried her off in a few days. Cf. L to M. Rosa: 16.10.'79 from Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni.

6 The school had opened on 10.9.1879 with 84 girls. Teachers: Sr. A. Damiana Giovenetti and Sr. A. Rosa Telleria (a Bolivian novice) for lessons, Sr. A. Livia Tallarini for needlework. Cf. L to M. Rosa of 20.11.'79 from Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni.

7 Sr. A. Rosa Telleria, cf. L 7, n. 8.

8 She had bought on credit the cloth she sent her, and the supplier wanted to be paid. Cf. L 27,3.

9 The removed President: Narciso Campero was favourable to the FSA. He was succeeded by Aniceto Arce, no less favourable than the first.

She accepts the postulant; let her send her off with the girl.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. The postulant and the sister arrived safely; they had a good journey and I hope the postulant will do well; she is a dear.

  2. So I very willingly accept the girl together with the Parish Priest's postulant, the one who is 40 years old. 1 She is a bit oldish, but what can I do? I need cooks. Everyone wants a good cook, and so I will satisfy them. Send them to me at once, so that before I leave I can clothe them with the others.

  3. Be sure not to come, because it is too cold;2 you can put them on the through train and they will arrive perfectly well; try to do it soon.

  4. Goodbye; thank you for everything you sent me, many thanks for all, and believe me yours for ever,

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The girl. She is 14, so she accepts her in order to prepare her for the postulancy. The 40-year-old postulant has good references. Sr. A. Crocifissa gives a positive opinion of both. Cf. L 21.1.'80 to M. Rosa.

2 Cf. L 15,4.

She will solve the financial problem. Let her accept the postulant.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line: I intend to write again to the Emaldi Co[mmission];1 keep your spirits up. Yes, accept the postulant and send her to me.2 As for coming there, rest assured I will do everything to grant your wish. Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa
